utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Two matters I want to deal with before we start -- in fact, I may be able to deal with three. The Trial Chamber has issued its decision now on the witnesses Burns and Philips. It was filed late yesterday. Not everyone may have a copy of it yet, but it will allow them to be added to the list of witnesses and to give evidence. It does make the point, however, that there remains the restriction on cross-examination on matters which might support the Defence position. It also says that once the Defence raise these matters with the Rule 70 provider, if there's any delay in them being dealt with, you will be permitted to re-call the witness in the course of the Defence case. You can read the detail for yourself. The important thing for the moment, though, is this, that if you do have points favourable to the Defence case which you wish to raise and for which authority is necessary from the Rule 70 provider, we would urge you to list these as soon as possible so that there remains the possibility of them being addressed by the Rule 70 provider between now and these witnesses giving evidence in the Prosecution case. And in the opinion of the Trial Chamber, what you need to do is identify issues, not lines of inquiry or lines of questioning that will be raised in court, but the particular issue on which you consider the witness should be able to give favourable evidence. The second matter is that there is a motion filed by Mr. Fila and Mr. Petrovic in relation to the evidence of Rugova. Now, Mr. Hannis, do you have any particular position on this?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, we're opposed to it. We think it's simply out of time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes. Your position isn't to say, Well, it's okay --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- it doesn't matter to us?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No. We're opposed. We asked for admission of all that evidence, that was granted, and we think it should remain, and if there were objections, they should have been raised at the time. We -- I had intended to file something today or tomorrow, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I think you should hold off for the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The Trial Chamber will consider the position today and we may be able to deal with this orally. The final matter is that your motion, Mr. Hannis, for further documents that relate to the evidence of Coo has been submitted, but there's another one yet to come. Now, we need a deadline for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Actually, in light of your remarks on Friday I had spent some time with Mr. Coo this weekend and we were actually having another go at his previous report, in light of your remarks about conclusions and opinions and speculation. And I think what we have now substantially removes all of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So your intention, if I can read between the lines there, is to present the remainder of the documents through him orally?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I was intending to offer that as a -- as a written statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah, but we need -- I mean, the statement didn't deal with authenticity and reliability; it was proceeding on the basis that these documents are here, here is what I make of them. And that doesn't address, for example, the large number of media reports on which undoubtedly evidence will be necessary to establish their authenticity.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And I thought you were going to give us a written filing to deal with the documents that you wanted to be part of his evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I guess I anticipated doing that with his new Coo-light report with those opinions and speculations removed, have him testify about that report, about his provenance report, where these documents come from and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: -- And why we think they're reliable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, is the report going to provide any more guidance to the Defence on the provenance, authenticity, and reliability of these documents, or have they got all they're going to get on that?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I believe they have that in the separate provenance report and the spreadsheet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So that leaves, then, the deadline for a separate report. When is that going to be available?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I was hoping that we could provide that to you on Wednesday and I wanted to seek some guidance from you. What we have done is gone through and blacked out everything, as we did before. That is not how I propose to submit it in its final form but I thought that might be helpful to the Court to see what's been removed and where it's been removed and the amount that's been removed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, then --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm not sure which is better for you to work with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- obviously, that can be done, but I have to say I don't feel encouraged of that in view of the general view we have with how riddled with comment the report is but you can't be faulted for trying, I suppose, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: All right, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But Wednesday would be helpful, because if it's not in satisfactory form and you're going to try yet again, you're running out of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I understand. I was of two minds about this when we discussed it with Mr. Coo this weekend, but upon looking at the first section that he did, I feel that we may have addressed Your Honour's concerns.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I hope that you do.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We can now have the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Dorovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The solemn declaration to speak the truth which you gave at the beginning of your evidence, naturally, continues to apply to that evidence today. You will now be cross-examined by those Defence counsel who wish to do so, and the first of these is Mr. Visnjic. Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Dorovic. Mr. Dorovic, I'm going to put a few questions to you. We are going to start with one of the topics that was dealt with last in your examination-in-chief yesterday, and it has to do with what you said about the National Council for Cooperation with the Tribunal and the Commission of the Army of Yugoslavia. The period that I'm going to talk about is actually the period between March and June 2003, and it starts with a letter of the Foreign Ministry of Serbia and Montenegro dated the 4th of March, 2003, which is 2685, Prosecution Exhibit 2685. Mr. Dorovic, that is one of the documents that I assume you submitted. My question in relation to this is the following: From this information provided by the Foreign Ministry of Serbia and Montenegro, the military commission was actually asked to give its opinion on the content and modalities of cooperation with the Tribunal. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The next document we have is Prosecution Exhibit 2684 dated the 12th of March, 2003. That is a letter of the Commission for Cooperation with The Hague Tribunal. That is precisely the opinion that we have been discussing. Since this is a rather lengthy document, I am going to deal with it in three parts. First of all, the commission says that the OTP seeks total access to the total archives. Secondly, the commission believes that the Prosecutor has to define the documentation that they seek and the reasons compelling them to seek these documents as relevant. And three, that this could imply a realistic possibility of providing data that would be relevant to criminal trials and that would be detrimental to national security. Mr. Dorovic, would this be a correct summary of the document that is before you in three points?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think you're right.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Where is my mistake?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You have too narrow a focus on the content. It cannot be dealt with that way. The commission provided its positions which really cannot be considered to be well-founded. In this segment, when you omit to mention that the commission also provides its positions, in that segment you are not being complete. So that is why I believe that you did not properly present the content of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: When you say "positions," can you indicate to me part of this document that is before you which shows these positions.

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, for example, in paragraph 3 there is reference to acts -- yes, I will try to speak properly. So I'm dealing with paragraph 3. It --

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: You said paragraph 3? What sentence are you referring to in paragraph 3?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Paragraph 3, presenting the position of the commission, that enabling the ICTY Prosecutor to have direct insight into all archived material in order to select what is and what is not relevant to the criminal proceedings, together with the physical access of the OTP staff to military facilities in which the archived material is kept implies the realistic possibility of data relevant to criminal proceedings leaking out. Well, you see, this was discussed by other people in the ministry as well. I'm talking about the analysis that was carried out in the ministry itself. Everybody ruled out the possibility of doing this realistically, of having data leaked out. I'll be very specific on this. Some of the members of the commission who analysed --

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dorovic, Mr. Dorovic, let me ask you specifically. Can you indicate to me a single sentence in this document is this implies the realistic possibility of leaks of confidential information that would be detrimental to national interest. Is that is the problem with this document?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it's other sentences as well. What I remember is that the commission for the most part - for the most part, I emphasise - gave negative positions with regard to all their proposals made by the OTP, giving, in the briefest possible terms, the reasons that we in the ministry consider to be quite unfounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dorovic --

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you wish to look at this document -- the sentence, rather.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: I am sorry for interrupting, but in this sentence, is there anything troublesome? Forget about what it is that you remember now and what you thought at the ministry. I'm asking you at this moment is there anything troublesome as you look at the document now?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am saying it was troublesome for us and unacceptable for us the position that there is a realistic possibility of leaks of confidential data. We did not see any such possibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I'm going to return to your document, and that is your response when you said "we in the ministry," that is the response of the legal department of the ministry dated the 3rd of June, 2003, Prosecution Exhibit 2675. In the opinion that you provided, on page 4 in paragraph 6 in the Serbian version, in the English version, page 6, the last paragraph, and page 7, paragraphs 1 and 2, you claimed that the commission in a calculated and erroneous manner analysed and monitored the rules by stating that the Prosecutor has to spell out his request and show quite specifically what it is that they seek. And this ties the hands of the Prosecutor. Am I right about this part?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that you actually interpreted the content of the text. Yes, that is what I wrote and that is that part of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Paragraph --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic, are you talking about the witness statement rather than the report? Because these pages on the report --

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 2675 is the document I'm referring to, Your Honour. I am sorry --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Ah.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] P2675. That is a document --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Oh, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- that the witness said yesterday that he wrote himself. A different person signed it, but the witness said that he is the person who wrote this document, so I would like to look at the findings with him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: At the end of page 5 of the same document and also on page 7 of the English interpretation, again I'm just summarising this, that these are arbitrary positions taken by the commission and as such, exceptionally detrimental to the interests of Serbia and Montenegro in the segment of cooperation with the Tribunal as a precondition for access to NATO and the European Union. Have I properly summarised that part of the document?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is the position.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But not only mine. It is the collective position and it is the position of the commission that preceded the analysis.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: But of course. You said that there were also some problems with regard to signing this document, that the chief didn't dare sign it, and ultimately it was signed by a person who was the acting chief. Did I understand you correctly?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You understood perfectly. The chief said that all of that was fine, that he personally thought so as well, but that he was afraid that the generals would destroy the entire administration and that he dare not sign this. And although he absolutely approved of every word and that he'd be glad to sign it, so the entire legal department and the entire ministry know about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Was this the time when the commission had already been abolished; am I right?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic, that commission works to the present day in a different form --

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: We'll get to that, but at that moment it had been abolished, the commission?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't think you're right. I think it hadn't been abolished. I think it had been working, and I think it never stopped working. It's been working until the present day. It works now.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: So you claim that this commission was never abolished?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not aware of it having been abolished. I think that it works today as well. I'm going to try to give you its present-day name. This is what it's called now: The Ministry of Defence Secretariat of the Ministry.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dorovic --

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Department for Cooperation with the International Criminal Tribunal and that is its third name. The core of the commission remained the same throughout.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Did you not write in paragraph 7: "Although the commission of the GSSM was abolished" --

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have a look at page 7 in the English translation. So can we just look at the bottom of page 7 now, and it's page 5, Article 7 in the Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Did you not write there that the commission had been dissolved?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It had never been dissolved, the commission.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Can you read paragraph 7, the first sentence.

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, that is just in one of the documents. That's what it said in just one of the documents, that it had been abolished and that it was pointless to discuss this. So this is just by way of a comment, differently put. The commission actually did exist, although formally somebody had been claiming that it did not exist. Even today there are people who will say that it does not exist.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Well, you claimed that it did not exist formally, at least that's what you wrote in paragraph 7?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that is what the secretariat said, that it was pointless to discuss all of this, because in actual fact, the commission no longer existed, although we all knew that it existed. And I claim with full responsibility even today that this commission does exist in a third form, a new form, with new members attached to it. It works and functions even today. It even --

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Let me interrupt you, Mr. Dorovic, and let us move on concerning the same document. Let us go back to my preceding question. When you say in this document that what is particularly detrimental to the total interests of Serbia and Montenegro and particularly in the segment of cooperation with the ICTY, as a precondition for accessing the EU and NATO. Am I right, Mr. Dorovic, that this is a political position that is being presented in a legal opinion?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're absolutely right. This is what can be construed.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: And this takes me back to another document that you showed us yesterday that the Prosecutor showed us yesterday in which you also provide a legal opinion and also put forth certain political positions or political interpretations. However, I'm going to ask you this: If we summarise this document, in your view, the obligation of the state would be this: To allow the OTP physical access to all the documents in the premises of the Army of Yugoslavia and Montenegro, physical access to the entire collections of documents. Am I right in saying this?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you may say so. The position of the working group with the ministry was such that we in the ministry and the army when it comes to the elucidation of the crimes that were committed and there were crimes and knew that there were crimes that there should be no secret that might rule access to such documents. In other words, we believed at the time that we actually did not have a valid reason, at least when it came to the protection of security of the state and the army which are the most sensitive segments, and this is what experts said, the result and the conclusion of the working group that I drafted, I accepted, I believe that it was grounded, it is something that I've always believed, when it came -- when it comes to crime, there should be no secret. We're talking about the gravest of crimes and we've never had any valid reason not to allow access to the documents calling upon the security of the state.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dorovic, I know that your answer will be negative, but still I can't stop myself from asking you. Are you aware of the contents of all the 17.000 documents that that commission had at its disposal at the time?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course not.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. My next question is this: Do you believe that the legal administration, if that is its position, might have had an insight into the boundaries of the interests of security? Let's leave aside the investigation of grave crimes. Do you think that the legal administration, which you indicated a minute ago, that the legal administration might be aware of the boundaries and the scope and limit of the data that might be detrimental to the national interests of Serbia and Montenegro?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic, Your Honours, maybe I would -- it would be good if I said that this document from the very beginning to the very end was adopted as the position of the Ministry of Defence. This document was submitted to the secretariat, and I claim this with full responsibility. The minister adopted this document, he signed it, and he sent it to other organs in the state. And as far as your question is concerned as to whether the commission is legally qualified to know that, I -- my answer will have to be yes. Under the rule - and I believe that you're familiar with the rule - the permission for providing data, if there is any fear that this may lead to disclosing confidential information, the Ministry of Defence and I, myself, in my career at least 30 times I've been in a position to prepare decisions for the minister himself and the decisions were made on requests for somebody to be exempted from keeping confidentiality of documents. When the --

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: I've asked you one thing. Is the legal administration authorised, and you said it is the minister who's authorised.

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The legal administration drafted regulations that regulated these matters and at the end of the day it is the legal administration that have always provided the last evaluation within the ministry before the minister issues a final decision on the exemption from -- the waiver from keeping confidential documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Can the legal administration then prepare a framework for a document?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If the legal administration provides an opinion, then the minister takes into account that professional opinion, and it's up to him whether he will sign or not. There are many things that he hasn't signed. There have been such cases when we submitted the document for his signature, he still did not sign, because he didn't want to sign.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: There is some mistake in translation, but I will leave it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Dorovic, would it mean anything to you if I told you that on the 18th of June, 2003, the Trial Chamber of this Tribunal in the third decision on Prosecution's motion according to Rule 54 issued an order and turned down the request by the Prosecution for physical access to the collections of documents, deeming that such physical access would be a search warrant as a matter of fact?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would never make such a decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've had a number of occasions to prepare decisions for others.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Are you aware of the fact that in another case a Trial Chamber of this Tribunal asked from a party in the proceedings to state concrete, contestable issues in the questions for which relevant documents were sought and also to state why the documents were relevant for these issues and likewise, to state the number of documents and the way they touch upon the contestable issues in the case?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is this a question, Mr. Visnjic?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic, you have to remember that that is a very unusual procedure here because states are expected to cooperate, and it's only in the event of a real genuine issue on cooperation -- over documents that this happens. It's not a question of documents only ever being handed over by a state because there's an application under Rule 54 bis. The Tribunal just couldn't function if that was how documents were meant to be regulated in their transmission to the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'm not talking about legal qualifications here; I'm just saying that the witness in this document that he drafted actually states that the previous positions that were confirmed by some decisions of this Tribunal are tendentious and that they were done in order to keep some documentation secret. And I'm just saying that the Trial Chambers of this Tribunal have confirmed such decisions, nothing else, and that in the document which he deems that it is tendentious, and the document number is 2684, P2684, that this document as a matter of fact contains a series of normal approaches that every serious organisation adopts in cooperating with another serious organisation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The two examples of decisions that you gave, are they both decisions in relation to applications for documents from Serbia and Montenegro?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the first example refers to a decision dated 18 June 2003. This is the: [In English] Motion for Orders Pursuant to Rule 54 Bis Against Serbia and Montenegro.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And is the other one also against Serbia and Montenegro?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And the other one is a decision in our proceedings against NATO and other members of NATO dated 23 March 2005.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, that one certainly relates to documents where there are particular issues relating to intelligence, as you know, and that's rather different from the question whether the archive in general should be opened up to the ICTY Prosecutor. Anyway, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dorovic, who was the minister of defence at the time when you drafted this document, in June 2003? Let me remind you, was it Boris Tadic at the time?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe so. Pavle had been killed, and after him it was General Ojdanic --

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: So Boris Tadic. We agree, don't we? And he is now the president of the state and the -- he commands the Army of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, according to the newly adopted constitution.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 51 you're saying that in the military commission documents are still being destroyed, that it is being done unofficially with the help of the centre for cooperation with the ICTY with the Ministry of Defence?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is exactly what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you have any reason to show why Boris Tadic, as the then-minister of defence, would be interested in covering up or falsifying documents?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If that is your question, Mr. Visnjic, let me put it this way. I have never said nor did I ever think that Mr. Tadic, as the president of state, would be organising this, but I would like to say quite openly something else. It is the ministry that is doing it, the current minister is -- who does it. This is my position. This is my experience. At the time, it was the associates of Mr. Tadic. Some of them were general who had been re-activated and re-instated. Let me give you some concrete examples. I was ordered to discard some documents --

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: You are going to provide concrete examples when the Prosecution asks you provide them with those. Let me ask you this: Did you inform anybody? Did you file a criminal report? Did you start any proceedings with regards to concealing and destroying documents?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I spoke to everybody who -- who had to be spoken to, first and foremost the legal administration and then Mr. Kovac as the chief of department. This was on the 6th of department -- 6th of February, 2002.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: So you've told us who it was. We will come to that later. Did you also file a report to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just a moment. The end of the answer when you were interrupted before the last answer was: "I was ordered to discard some documents." Now, tell us about the circumstances in which that happened.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For example, the county court from Split called witnesses. We had witnesses. I organised a meeting with them, and we could send them over there, but then from the General Staff -- actually, from the secretariat it was ordered to us to prepare information that the access to witness was not possible. That's one example. Another example, I worked with two people on the request of the Federal Ministry for Foreign Affairs and the request was to return money and valuables to some people in Slavonia, more specifically near Vukovar. We knew --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. -- sorry, Mr. Dorovic, the -- this trial isn't about cooperation with Split and it's not about cooperation or otherwise with Slavonia. I was more interested in an example which I thought you were going to give of being ordered to discard documents that might be relevant to the ICTY. Now, is there no such example?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Precisely these documents were requested about some money that had been seized in the vicinity of Vukovar and whether this had been done by this particular group, the group of military security that was operational on the ground over there. We were supposed to submit --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We're not dealing with Vukovar either, Mr. Dorovic. So let's move on, Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dorovic, if somebody committed a crime of the sort you are describing - I'm asking you as an expert and somebody who works with the Ministry of Defence - would it be something that would be prosecuted by the military prosecutor, if this is done by a serviceman should it be the military prosecutor who should have a prosecute that?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As a prosecutor I insisted on that; that is why I was removed from my position.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: We will come to that. I'm just asking you for your opinion.

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The destruction of official documents is a crime.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Didn't you say yesterday that -- that a person whom you hold in very high esteem, Nikola Petkovic, was the supreme military prosecutor at the time these things happened? Am I right?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is what I said, and that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Am I right in saying that Nikola Petkovic is one of the individuals for whom you claim that he is an excellent legal expert and that he can't be influenced by others?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not say that he couldn't be influenced by others. Unfortunately, he was prevented from doing his job and I believe that you know it very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: I don't, no.

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know and everybody in the army knows that it is a general piece of knowledge that his hands were tied and that he was prevented from doing his job properly.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: And this was done by the security service, the military security service, am I right, if you say that his hands were tied by somebody?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It sounds a bit cynical, at least to me, but I will say yes, they were the ones who tied his hands. Either him or I could not work in any serious proceedings. Mr. Visnjic, I can tell you about mine and Petkovic's joint experience in elucidating some very serious crimes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dorovic, I would like to hear something about your experience when I ask you about your experience, and as for Petkovic, we will call him and he will talk about his experience.

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm talking about my experience from the time when he was my boss and he gave me tasks and then explained to me that he had given them to me because an assumption was that if I, as a stubborn person that I am, come to a certain result with his support and we had some concrete cases in which he said lucky we are doing this to no avail, we cannot prosecute, they did it, they don't allow us to investigate.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Mr. Dorovic, on several occasions in newspapers you provided comments on Milosevic's trial. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, you are not right. The only article is relative to General Radomir Gojovic, my former boss, a person who humiliated and maltreated me. He almost ruined me. And here from the Tribunal's courtroom he smeared me and he belittled my name.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: I only asked you a question. I'm not right. This is the one and only article and the number of the Exhibit is P2673. Therefore, you were in conflict with Mr. Gojkovic, even before this article was published, because of some court proceedings. Now I should like you to read paragraph 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please enlarge the left middle partly of the article a bit down, please. Yes, just beneath this headline "permanently unworthy."

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Can you read the first paragraph beneath that headline, since it's your article.

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course. "General Gojovic has in the course of long-standing and" -- let me repeat. "In the course of his long-lasting and diligent work within the illegal commission of the General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia for the Cooperation with The Hague Tribunal, General Gojovic reviewed, and who knows what else he did, to many of the 17.000 documents that the commission had in their unlawful possession. Therefore, Gojovic's testimony as well as possible future testimonies of the other members of this unlawful commission must be evaluated from that point of view as well. Therefore, Gojovic does not speak about matters of personal knowledge, rather he interprets documents that are of an otherwise suspicious content made by other persons. Therefore, Gojovic appears less as a real witness and more as a partial quasi expert witness."

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Yesterday you spoke about and interpreted documents drafted by other persons?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I analysed them with the permission of the Court. Yes, I did, some of the documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Were you not, therefore, in relation to these documents not a real witness but as some sort of an expert witness? And I will not use the terms you used in your article.

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic, I was given this role by the Court. I was asked to comment on certain documents and I did that. It is my personal conviction that as a lawyer, I am able to provide comments. Generally speaking, I do have a certain position about all these documents and I gave my position with the permission of the Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: I understand that, but wasn't that the case, in fact, with Mr. Gojovic as well, who was asked to provide comments on some documents?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe I was referring to something quite different here. He gave his comments on the documents from a third party. My comments before this Tribunal were of a different nature. I spoke of documents being modified back home, and that's quite a different matter. If you believe, however, that I am a quasi expert witness --

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: No, no. I believe that Petkovic was not a quasi expert witness and I believe that you wrote this because you have been at loggerheads with him for years over a different proceedings, and I believe that the persons you come into conflict, you tend to demean them in any possible way you can.

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, that is not true. Just as I am keen to commend persons and give them credit, well and one of them of course is Petkovic, whose hands were tied. You will remember that I spoke about many other of my superior officers favourably. Every person among them who spoke their mind were driven away. I had occasion to meet many brave, honest people who were driven out of the army for speaking out. It wasn't by chance that the bar association excluded Gojovic from their membership, and this wasn't done pursuant to a request coming from me but from other quarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Let us not go into other matters concerning Mr. Gojovic, who is a lawyer and you very well know that. He wasn't expelled from the bar association and you know that. He wasn't disbarred.

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I do know for a fact that he was disbarred. There is a decision to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: You know very well, Mr. Dorovic, that Mr. Gojovic is a lawyer and that the decision you are referring to was rescinded in the second instance.

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No -- well, I don't know about that. I only know that he was disbarred.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: But you don't know about the further developments concerning that matter?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I hear about that for the first time now. It's news to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Very well. Let me ask you about one section of this document. No. I'll move on. Please, tell me, Dopudja, the person who signed the earlier document on behalf of the Ministry of Defence, was he your superior ever? Am I right?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: But he signed the document you drafted; am I right?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely. You can see that on the document, it bears his signature, but this is the document of the legal administration or department and the ministry. I merely drafted the document and it was accepted. It was quite unfortunate that he had to do that. It would have been proper for the chief to have done that, and I told you that he didn't muster up the courage to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: And this person, Dopudja, Lieutenant-Colonel Dusko Dopudja, you said that he was also the person cooperating with the security organ of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, everybody knows about that. He was brought over from Ruma for that purpose precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Am I right in saying that you made the same claims in relation to a person called Mihaljovic?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Milovan Mihaljovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I made such claims but he himself professed as much.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: I put to you that you wrote a series of representations, petitions, and criminal reports against persons you came into conflict with, where you referred to them as a rabbit in uniform, security officers, cowards?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do recognise there Colonel Mihaljovic and Dopudja. Besides, those were the terms that they used to refer to themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have P2735 called up, please, page 1 in the Serbian version, page 2 in the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: This is your letter, Mr. Dorovic, to the federal defence minister dating from September 2001. I'm waiting for the document to appear on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 1 of the Serbian text, the bottom half of it, and in the English, page 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Let us not read the entire text. I will only read the bottom part under D where it says: "The gravest violations of procedure carried out by Colonel Domindza in order to frighten the rabbit in the uniform was in order to make him --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter couldn't catch up with the witness -- with the counsel, couldn't find the portion.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: I want to ask you, Colonel Mihailov was your superior, wasn't he? ?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was the acting chief of department for regulations, but he was never appointed.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Was Colonel Mihajlovic your superior at any point in your career?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Formally, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: And de facto?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in some specific situations because in the army you always have a superior/subordinate relationship.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You mentioned the name of Zivadinovic and you said that person was called Zivadinovski. Here you call Colonel Mihaljovic as Mihailov. Are you calling them Zivadinovski and Mihailov as a disparaging term?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What is the drift of your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: I am just reading what you're saying.

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's the way it was typed. Mihaljovic is Mihaljovic and Zivadinovski was indeed Zivadinovski. As long as I know him, he's always been Mihaljovic, and everybody in the army will tell you that Zivadinovski is called Zivadinovski.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: So you believe, in fact, that his name was misprinted here as Mihaljovic, should be Mihaljovic?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Milovan Mihaljovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: And why do you repeat the same mistake on the next page, where you mention him again as saying that they should re-consider their decisions?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. That's the way it was printed.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: And when you say Colonel Domindza, does that in fact refer to Colonel Dopudja?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: So why are you calling him Domindza?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. It was a typo.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dorovic, this letter was sent to the defence minister. I believe that in this letter you deliberately changed Colonel Dopudja's name into this disparaging name of Domindza and you deliberately changed Colonel Mihaljovic's name into Colonel Mihailov and you are deliberately slinging offences at these persons, especially when you refer to them as "Zuler." What does a "Zuler" mean, Mr. Dorovic?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'll tell you frankly. There is a biography concerning General Gojovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Leave that aside. What does Zuler mean?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It means -- it's a term for a non-commissioned officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: What does Domindza mean?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: If we knock off "d-o" what would the rest of the word mean?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean in gypsy language?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Yes. If you know that's it's a gypsy-like term, then you know what it means.

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: And we will both agree that it's a harshly derogatory term?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it could be.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: And it's the same type of word that was sent by your deputy and then you drove him away in Pristina. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not right.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: What is not right, that it's not the same word or that you did not, in fact, punch him in the head?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, none of that is true. He did not address me -- address me with this word; rather, he kept on offending me throughout the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Well -- very well, if you claim that you did not, in fact, utter the word, we have that in the transcript and we shall see.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 27, line 6, instead of: "Then you drove him away in Pristina," it should say that: "You punched him in the head in Pristina" -- "kicked him in the head," rather.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's not true. After six hearings, they dropped their charges. It's a lie.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Believe me, Mr. Dorovic, we will be discussing this matter later. This Colonel Mihailov or Mihaljovic, who you say you did not refer to in derogatory terms, apart from saying that he cowered down like a frightened rabbit, when you needed him to appear as a witness in your case --

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please call up Exhibit P2701, page 8 in the Serbian version.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dorovic, for your information, this is your request for an investigation, for an inquiry, against Milovic, Miladinovic, and Gojovic, and in the list of witnesses you were tendering, the last witness on the list is Milovan Mihaljovic, honourable judge of the supreme military court. Mr. Dorovic, is that the same person you referred to in your earlier text as rabbit, cooperating with the security service?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's the same person, but when I said "honourable," I, in fact, meant dishonourable, because such a person should not be a civil servant, let alone a judge.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Well, you should [as interpreted] mince your words. When you say say honourable, you should then mean honourable; dishonourable should mean dishonourable.

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know what I mean when I write something down.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: I'm just waiting for interpretation. Mr. Dorovic, how can you call a person you consider dishonourable as a witness?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In order for him to explain his dirty role, in order for everyone else to see how full of blemishes he is. Besides, why did he leave the service? Why didn't he stay? All of us know what Milovan Mihaljovic is, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Let us go over to paragraphs 13 to 16. We are moving on to matters that might be connected with this case. Mr. Dorovic, in paragraphs 13 through 16 of your statement there is mention of the case involving Australians who were arrested. This is one of the cases you said you had worked on at the time you were a prosecutor in Belgrade. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to say that I refused to be involved in that case. I spoke about the case only in view of the pressures put upon me to falsely accuse my subordinate.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: You say that in the month of May of 1999, the top leadership decided that these two persons from Australia who were, according to you, in fact, arrested in May to present them as special representatives of NATO forces who were infiltrated in order to assassinate Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was what General Obrencevic told me, because he wanted me to falsely accuse Milovan Mihaljovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Very well. Do you know that these two Australians were arrested in late March 1999 on the border crossing with Croatia?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please call up P -- 3D526. Your Honour, could the content of this document please be interpreted only in terms of the date and the time-period that is described here. Please do not look at its content as to whether they were spies or not, because I believe that this is fully irrelevant as far as this case is concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: So we have this information that two Australian citizens were arrested in March 1999. Mr. Dorovic, do you know --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic, how we treat it will depend on the questions asked, and it may be that you are opening up a line for re-examination. I don't know. But we can't necessarily prevent that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, no, I'm just drawing your attention to the fact that I am not trying to prove anything through this document which is not the object of my cross-examination, but of course it's up to the Prosecutor what they are going to do with this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Do you know that as far back as mid-April the Australian Embassy was informed about this and that the case was publicised in the world in the same period?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know. I really don't know whether we're talking about the same persons. I bear in mind the name of a man whose name I wrote down as told to me by General Obrencevic. If you wish, in my war diary I can find the date when I was given this order. I was asked to do this in May, and I have the name of this one journalist written down. Unfortunately, I don't speak English. I don't even know how to pronounce their names properly. I just know that this man is John Peter or Pater or whatever you pronounce his name and there's this third name. I pronounce it as Schnitzel, Schnatzel, something like that, but I have it written down in my war diary in the English language. I was asked only to falsely accuse Milovan Radovanovic my deputy. I never actually had this case. It was brought to me so that I would be forced to bring these false charges; I refused. Everything I said is actually by way of an explanation as to how I was being coerced into doing something. So that is the third reason why I --

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dorovic, Mr. Dorovic, let me put short questions and you give me short answers.

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: So you're telling me now that they were not Australians and there was not two of them, there was one of them.

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please don't. I am saying that these were two persons, that one person's name is what I told you just now and the other person's name, I don't know. I am saying that they were held in different locations, several places, and I'm saying that another prosecutor dealt with this case and the court did, too and that I was just asked to falsely accuse my deputy of having betrayed information --

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Again I have to interrupt you. You told me now that in actual fact, there were two persons involved?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: And they were Australians?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what I wrote down and that is what General Obrencevic said to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If I tell you that there are no two other Australians arrested in Serbia in I don't know how many years, except for these two men, can we agree then that it's probably those two persons who are mentioned here in this statement that we're talking about?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If that is really the case, then there is no other option. It would have been to be these people.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: If I tell you now that the Australian Embassy in mid-April was informed about this case and that in April Serbian Radio Television -- let me just refer you to the actual page. The end of this page and the beginning of the next page. So state television broadcast that Major Steve Pratt was involved in this agent network and that it was cut off, and if I tell you that Malcolm Fraser at the end of April - and Malcolm Fraser was the former Australian Prime Minister - and he visited these two persons who were detained and he informed the world public about the details of the charges brought against them, and this is on page 2 of this document, paragraphs 4 and 5. And if I tell you that the document that I'm reading all of this from was made public, that is 3D526, on the 29th of April, 1999. Mr. Dorovic, who could decide to construe this kind of thing, after all of this to make a claim that in mid-May somebody would think of accusing them as NATO special agents who were infiltrated in order to assassinate Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic, I don't understand what it is that you are talking about. I don't know about any of these names. I can explain to you what it was that I had been saying. I was asked to perjure myself, to give false testimony. My then-deputy -- about him, that I had betrayed information --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Dorovic, we know the story as you've given it already, but your statement says: "One day in May 1999 the military security arrested two journalists from Australia." And Mr. Visnjic is -- has invited you to concentrate on the timing and is showing you a document which indicates that this was already public in April, and he's asking you to explain why you said they were arrested in May. That's all.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because in May, sometime between the 1st and the 10th of May, I was told that this had to do with two Australian journalists and that my deputy had disclosed information as to where it was that he -- that they were. And that on the 10th of May, my deputy was arrested and I was asked to present in writing that he had had documents, and then the conclusion would be drawn that he could have betrayed these documents, or rather, this information. And I said that in our office of the prosecutor we did not have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We've got all that. Do you now accept that you may be wrong when you say that it was in May that the military security arrested the journalists?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that in May -- well, obviously I made a mistake in the dates. But I was asked to do all of this in May; that is what I was talking about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We understand that. And if you concentrate on things like that, explaining when you were asked that and that that really may be a different time from the arrest, we'll make some progress. Please don't fight the battles you fought earlier by setting everything out in writing for us. Concentrate on the questions you're being asked and answer these specific questions; that's how we'll make progress here. Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dorovic, I will try to be more specific. Do you know that before this Tribunal in this case General Vasiljevic testified --

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The page reference is 8901, Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: And that General Vasiljevic said that there were no secret prisons that these persons were in Ustanicka Street in Belgrade, that the security service did not bring any pressure to bear on the judicial organs, especially not in relation to this case, and that no efforts were made to link them up with any kind of attempt to assassinate anyone. Quite simply, they were charged and later convicted of espionage. Do you know about that, Mr. Dorovic?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the first time I hear of this. I was in Ustanicka if you are referring to Ustanicka 29, the facility there --

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: No, Mr. Dorovic, I asked you whether you know that Vasiljevic testified before this Tribunal and said that; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know about it. This is the first time I hear of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Now, in your statement you say that your deputy, Radovanovic, allegedly disclosed a secret to Dragoljub Stankovic. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is what General Obrencevic claimed, and I was asked to falsely -- accused --

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: I'm just asking you if I am right on this, yes or no.

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you know what, you take things out of context.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: I'm just leading you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just answer the question you're asked. We'll decide about the context; you will not run this court. Do you understand that? You may be used to running courts elsewhere, but in this court you will please follow the procedure that we follow. Answer the specific questions you're being asked, please. Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Yes or no, am I right if I say that it is your claim that Radovancevic [as interpreted] allegedly disclosed secrets to Stankovic?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Please don't answer that question. Mr. Visnjic, it really is a silly question to ask, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You're asking for trouble because the answer is in the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Yes, okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dorovic, let's try to deal with it this way. Is Dragoljub Stankovic the same person who is now deputy prosecutor for war crimes in Serbia?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what position he holds now, Dragoljub Stankovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: But he did work in the office of the prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, before the war, I was told that he was Radovanovic's deputy. I actually first met Radovanovic as one of my deputies on the 24th of March. I did not know either one of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: All right. Do you know that -- well, if you didn't know then perhaps Radovanovic told you this. Do you know that Stankovic and Radovanovic were very close? Perhaps they were even the best of friends?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I need 3D537, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know about that. I really had no occasion to --

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: At the time when you gave this statement, and that was September 2006, Radovanovic was no longer alive.

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know, I know, I saw the obituary. I knew that he died therefore.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dorovic, we talked to Dragoljub Stankovic, who is currently the deputy prosecutor for war crimes of the Republic of Serbia. And in his statement, which is 3D537, on page 1, paragraph 4, says the following: "I am surprised and this is the first time I hear that the late Radovanovic had such problems with the military prosecutor. I'm sure that he would have told me immediately about it during the bombing. On the assumption that he was afraid about this for some reason, he certainly would have told me about it after the bombing campaign, because afterwards we continued being the same kind of friends." Mr. Dorovic, in your statement you said that Radovanovic knew about these proceedings that had been initiated against him and that he thanked you for the fact that you didn't want to testify against him.

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Everybody in my office knows about that, in the prosecutor's office, or everybody in the military court knows about that. Radovanovic knows about that, too, because on the day of the celebration in front of about 60 people he took my right hand and he said that his fate and the fate of his family is in my hands. He cried and he asked me to help him. At that moment, the security organs took me away --

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: We'll get to that. We'll get to the security organs. Mr. Dorovic, I'm proceeding --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: In fairness, Mr. Visnjic, what you were getting there was an explanation of how the witness can tell that he -- that Radovanovic knew exactly what was going on. Anyway, it probably was enough, but it was an answer that was specifically related to the question, in this instance.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Dorovic, I'll just refer to two other parts in Dragoljub Stankovic's statement. The scenario written in the statement is one that I recognise as identical to what happened to Radovanovic -- the late Radovanovic last year, he's referring to 2006, when he was accused of disclosing official secrets. Unfortunately, he could not take the proceedings, and he died on account of that.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters cannot find the reference in the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: And the last sentence: "Therefore," --

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is on the second page in the English text.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: "It is not only what Dorovic said is incorrect, but it is not clear at all why he is linking me to this. In my opinion, this is a totally fabricated thing. I repeat that Radovanovic and I were friends and this was a generally known fact in Belgrade, and it is only in that context that I could have been mentioned." Mr. Dorovic, do you allow for this possibility, that you confused what had happened and that you put prosecutor Radovanovic in the context of something that had not actually happened in 1999?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic, that question is offensive, as a matter of fact. I repeat to you that 60 persons saw this dirty scenario in which I was expected to immediately sign a statement to the effect that I had given documents to Radovanovic and that he had most probably handed them over to someone. This third party was supposed to be Stankovic, and it is General Obrencevic who asked me to do that. General Gojkovic asked me to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dorovic, you are ruling out that possible, right, that is a sufficient answer. Thank you. Now we are going back to the security organs who were bringing this pressure to bear on --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Again, the fact that they were friendly, Mr. Visnjic, surely makes it even more likely that this might happen. We're talking about an instruction to frame somebody because he had dealings with someone else. And if it turns out that that someone else was a friend, does that not make it more likely?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, there are two possible options: Either that it really happened and Stankovic would have to know about it; or that an attempt was made to frame him, which is a completely different option. And now I'm going to explore that a bit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is that not -- is that not the witness's evidence, that this was all a fiction? He was being instructed to prosecute something that didn't happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. The witness did not rule out that possibility at all, that this had not happened. As to whether it had happened and whether this fiction or this false accusation could be fabricated at that moment, and that moment is mid-May 1999, I leave that for you to assess in relation to the previous documents when I set the time foundation as to when things were happening.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just -- whether Radovanovic actually told Stankovic anything or gave him information, or whether he didn't, does it make any difference to -- or is it going to help us on the question of whether this witness was asked to proceed on a false allegation about handing over the case to him?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If the allegation was false, then this is an entirely different topic. If the allegation was true and the witness was asked to testify against a colleague, he could not have been the judge of that at the moment. He was working on the second-hand information. The witness did not -- was not in a position to know whether the allegation was false or true.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am convinced that it was a false allegation. It was fabricated. The situation was fabricated just for him to be arrested --

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If the situation had been constructed, Stankovic should have been in the loop.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] However, let's go back to something else. Let's move forward.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dorovic, you are saying that a group of people threatened you. You called them members of the security.

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they were in the security administration in the security department of the 1st Army. Sukla -- Sinisa Kutlaca -- Kracun was for the security administration, Bratislav, Bratso, Stamenkovic was the -- from the security administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Let's go back to something.

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Zigic Branko Djokanovic [as interpreted] -- 16 people, and I repeat 60 people were there. They knew of all of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: This is chaos. You have to slow down. You're both speaking the same language. It has to be interpreted, therefore there must be a pause between the question and the answer. So please slow down generally.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dorovic, if I'm asking you whether a group threatened you, your answer should be yes or no and then I'll go on asking you questions.

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Now, you have told us that in that group, and in the statement you also stated that in that group was a person whom you identified as Lieutenant-Colonel Kracun; am I right?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you are. He was there. That's what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. My next question is this --

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to call up 3D527, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Do you know that the person whom you identified as Lieutenant-Colonel Kracun is not an active officer but a civilian person serving with the Army of Yugoslavia and he could not be a lieutenant-colonel as such? Are you aware of that fact?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my view, he was lieutenant-colonel. I was with him. He was a colonel; that's how he introduced himself to me and that's what everybody addressed him as.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we go to page 2 of this exhibit in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Do you know that this person never worked as a security organ, either in the Ministry of Defence or in the General Staff?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not true. Everybody knows Kracun.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know that in the statement that we took from him - and the exhibit number is 3D527 - Kracun claims that the Australians were detained in a military investigation prison? ?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know that. I've already told you that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: However, you know that they were detained in several such prisons?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is what General Obrencevic told me.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know that this person denies ever having contacted you or putting pressure on you on these grounds?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know that. He lies if he says that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: You still claim that all that was happening happened in the first half of May, around the 10th of May?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 10th of May, the day of the military judiciary celebration day.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: This person, Kracun, whom you know as a lieutenant-colonel or colonel, you think that he may be tied to the case of the alleged blackmail of Albanians regarding their possible service in the army?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not tying him up with that. I am claiming that he was together with the others whom I named. They were all in civilian clothes, and these persons that I've already mentioned today were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Do we agree that with regard to this case of blackmailing Albanian recruits or military conscripts, as you called them --

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, conscripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: -- could it be true that Branko Zigic, as the chief of the security service of the command of the Belgrade army district, should know before you that there was such an organised blackmail by virtue of his position?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this would only be natural.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Is it true that by virtue of the matter you could not be aware of this because the security service should submit --

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: So we agree that the security service, according to the rules, should be aware of the case before it reaches your hand?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: So much more so because they were the ones who organised everything with their associates, and some of them did that. Some of them were involved. I don't know whether you're referring to anybody specific.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: I'm referring to the service, Zigic, and his position.

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is what the case was. This is the case with a written trail, with documents which say that certain members of the military security were in that network. I was asked to arrest Lieutenant-Colonel Rackovic and Lieutenant-Colonel Aleksic. And in that network -- in that network there were also some security organs and a problem started at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: We have a problem with the interpretation --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic, which paragraph of the statement does this relate to?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this is the case of blackmailing Albanian -- 10, paragraph 10.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And what is your problem with the interpretation?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I just wanted the gentleman to slow down; that's why I said we had problems with interpretation, that the interpreters could not follow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dorovic, now you have provided us with the names Rackovic and Aleksic?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Rackovic, the military department Novi Belgrade, and Aleksic from the military department in Zemun. And if I remember it well, the same departments.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: In your statement under item 10 you say that a person called Strunjas from the General Staff was at the head of that network?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is not just any Strunjas.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Am I right?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you're absolutely right.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Do you know his name?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know, unfortunately.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: We'll come to that Strunjas anyway but before that I would like to show you what Branko Zigic has to say?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Exhibit Number 3D528, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You've done it earlier than this, counsel. Why do you need to show the exhibit number of the statement and show the statement? Why don't you just ask the relevant question that arises from it?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I agree, Your Honour. I have already asked questions based on the statement actually --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Is there a question or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Just bear in mind for a moment, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Please be patient.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
