utterances.text: Mr. Dorovic, we have tried to conduct an investigation, and the only Strunjas that exists in the General Staff is a certain Colonel Djordjije Strunjas. Exhibit Number 3D528 testifies to that. This person obviously doesn't know anything about that, and during the war he was in Montenegro. He was in the command of the navy and he was affiliated with the staff duties.

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I left for Kosovo later on myself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: These names are spelled quite differently --

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What is the correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Djordjije Strunjas, S-t-r-u-n-j-a-s, Exhibit Number 3D529. And again I spell the name, S-t-r-u-n-j-a-s. And the second one we mentioned is Branko Zigic. This is spelled correctly, and the exhibit number is 3D528. I would like to call up 3D529.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dorovic, you actually don't know the name of this man, Strunjas, who according to you was the organiser of this large network?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that he was a colonel from the General Staff and that together with him was a certain Colonel Stojkovic from the administration of the defence of the city of Belgrade. I was given a task from General Obrencevic to personally carry out an investigation. I was assigned four police officers. I went personally to the military department in Novi Belgrade, and then to Zemun. And my specific task was to interview Colonels Rackovic and Aleksic from these two respective military departments. After that, when I returned and when I reported to General Obrencevic, I was ordered to -- to talk to Branko Zigic, Colonel Zigic, and he told me that the best thing for me would be to forget all about this case or otherwise something bad would happen to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: And in this group that was surrounding this case, you say that Kracun was also part of that and you say that he was a colonel?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I am saying is that they came to see me on that occasion. All the organs of security - that's what we called them - all the officers, there would be three in every military department. I remember Pavlovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you about Kracun. Was he there?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Kracun was there in civilian clothes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: And what was his position or function? He was a security organ in the military department?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I am saying all this time and I have repeated it today that Kracun was from the security administration. I don't know how many times I have to repeat this.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: You say in your statement that Kracun was from the General Staff and the Ministry of Defence.

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He can't be from both things. He was from the security administration of the Ministry of Defence, the Ministry of Defence. That's what I said, and Sinisa Kutlaca was from the department --

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: I'm reading your statement, paragraph 15, which says: "I left my office and was met by members of the security organs of the General Staff, Lieutenant Kutlaca, Lieutenant-Colonel Kracun, and Lieutenant-Colonel Stamekovic," are these your words?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, those are my words.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: A lot of that evidence was about the Albanian blackmail case. And then you asked a question: In this group that was surrounding this case you say that Kracun was also part of that. Do we link this to the case of Radovanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A link should be made in the sense that the witness just summarily mentions names of the persons that -- whose names occurred to him at the time with every case. Later on we will present evidence about Kracun's position --

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- and whether he could at all be involved in this case of blackmail.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I understand that, but what I'm not understanding is whether Kracun was involved in any way in the case relating to the Albanian blackmail. Ms. Moeller.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Your Honours, may I clarify that and also comment. This comment that the witness just arbitrarily puts names, I object to that. In paragraph 11 which deals with the blackmailing event, he mentions Colonel Kracun, and in --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: -- paragraph 15 of the statement --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: -- which relates to the other event, he also mentions him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I appreciate the -- I was confining my attention, regrettably, to paragraph 10 and hadn't moved on to 11, but I see that the names are there, in fact. Thank you very much. Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: And finally, Mr. Dorovic, let me tell you what Colonel Strunjas said in his statement. He said that he's surprised and that he is prepared to face everybody that Dorovic mentions and who were allegedly part of the blackmailing network. And he says that what you say about him is simply not true. I move on to another topic that you describe. This is the case Tijanic, this is one of the cases you worked on. In paragraph 20 you say --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Before you -- you can do that after the break. Mr. Visnjic, what you've just done is just quite unnecessary and inappropriate. We're not here to hear the statements of your witnesses through your mouths at this stage. I have to question why you do this. Is it for some sort of publicity reason? Because it's certainly not an appropriate part of the process that we are going through here. So we'll have a break. We need to break at this stage, as we did yesterday, Mr. Dorovic. The usher will show you where to go, and we will resume at 11.15.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Dorovic, or rather --

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have 3D530 called up, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dorovic, could you please refresh your memories concerning the Tijanic case. In paragraph 20 of your statement you state that the investigation in this case was handed over to the investigating magistrate Katanic. You had cooperation with the investigating magistrate during the war, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He was one of the investigating magistrates there.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Was your cooperation good?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm not sure I would put it that way. He was a junior colleague only starting in his clear, and this was the only case I had personal dealings with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: You see, in your statement you claim that General --

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Milos Gojkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Yes, Milos Gojkovic put pressure to bear on him.

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes,. President of the Supreme Court, he ordered him to abort his investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Katanic was indeed in charge of this case, Mr. Dorovic, and I'm just putting this to you now. I don't want to go into any further details. He says that, in fact, detention was ordered in that case and that in the beginning, the case seemed to be handled -- or rather,"seemed to be serious and this is in paragraph 5 of his statement, that after certain investigation measures were taken, in my view, these were -- this was a person with strictly restricted psychological abilities, and he's referring to Mr. Tijanic, and nobody seems to have noticed this fact." And finally he says that: Because of the poor state in which the case was, upon the request of the defence the detention was cancelled and the case was aborted. Is this something that is consistent with your memory?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I went to Kosovo later on and I wasn't really kept abreast of the matter later on. I know how the case was started, and I know that it was a very difficult case for me involving, I should say, hundreds of documents in evidence with great amounts of receipts concerning confiscated items. I know that I was asked to review all the documents immediately, and it was Nikola Petkovic himself who helped me, professionally speaking, in my work. I worked based on his verbal instructions, and as problems emerged according to the orders -- I worked according to the orders of General Obrencevic. I tried to resist pressure and I hoped that I was doing my job properly. At any rate, this was a case dealt by the court and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Dorovic, what is your basis for saying that Gojkovic ordered him to carry out the investigation in such a way as to terminate it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this because General Gojkovic, the president of the supreme military court, and General Obrencevic, military prosecutor -- the chief military prosecutor, came to see me personally to try and convince me to drop charges as military prosecutor. I refused to do that. This meeting was witnessed by other persons. I remember that there was Major Djakonovic from the police force. He was given a police unit to secure the building, and Colonel Branko Zigic was there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We have all that in your statement. My question is a specific one. What is your basis for saying that Gojkovic ordered Katanic to carry out the investigation in such a way as to terminate it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The fact that General Gojkovic, later on when I returned from the war in Kosovo, told me, Well, you see, this is the way big-headed people fare and because of my actions I fared the way I did. I have to tell you that it's the generals who make decisions. He ordered Aleksander Tijanic -- or rather Katanic, the -- the investigating magistrate, to do that. Milos Gojkovic told me so personally in the presence of others and the Judge Katanic told me that as well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, now we're getting closer to the answer to the question. Why can't you just concentrate on the question? Are you now saying that Gojkovic told you that he told Katanic to carry out the investigation in such a way as to terminate it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Gojkovic told me that in the presence of others, and Aleksandar Katanic also told me that he was categorically asked to terminate the case and that's what he did. Investigating Judge Katanic told me that as well. They can say whatever they want. I'm saying you what I know, and my prosecutors knew that as well, because we had a great amount of work --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Dorovic, just answer my questions, please, and we'll maybe make some progress. Who were the people present when Gojkovic told you this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My deputies were. There was some administration staff there as well. There was the president of the court. I believe there was some others still, but I can vouch for these because all of us, especially the court, were very disappointed. But we were told that the Supreme Court ordered this and we complied --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I don't think I am going to be prepared to tell you again just to answer the questions I'm asking you and then we will make progress. Now, what was the name of the president of the court?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Captain First Class Korolija.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And the deputies, what were their names?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My deputies were Brano, Branislav, Turkovic, he was one of the deputies, Milan Radovanovic, Lepetic -- Branko Lepetic, Nemanja Vukotic, he was my deputy for a while and then spent some time in the navy and then came back --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm only interested to know the names of the deputies who were present when Gojkovic told you that he had ordered the termination of this investigation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, the three persons I mentioned, I know about them for a fact, because they assisted me in my work. Svetislav Postic was also there. He was from the prosecutor's office that was our superior, the president of the court and Katanic. Because we tried to persuade Postic as representative of the supreme military prosecutor's office that we should not discredit ourselves by such conduct. We can't arrest a person and then release him if we know that he had concealed a great amount of assets.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Have you difficulty understanding the concept of answering the particular question that I ask you? Does that cause you a particular problem?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I thought that I had answered the question. I listed the names of the persons who were present. I didn't mention --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You've answered it in a way that causes confusion, because we have four assistants and you say that three were present. So could you tell us who the three deputies were who were present when this was said.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've already mentioned them, Milan Radovanovic, Branko Lepetic, and Nemanja Vukotic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And therefore, Turkovic was not --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Branislav, Brano, Turkovic, he was also present. He had specific tasks to deal with in obtaining documents from security organs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, after your ruling, I will only refer the entire Chamber to the statement by Katanic, 3D530, which I previously referred to.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dorovic --

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I am told by my colleague Cepic that it is confirmed that Katanic was present at this meeting that the witness mentioned a while ago when pressure was brought to bear upon him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We've got that, but he's not a deputy prosecutor at that stage. That's -- I was interested in the names of the three deputy prosecutors that were there and it's still not been clearly answered. But never mind, let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dorovic, we are nearing the time when you left for Kosovo. We will now be dealing with the Stosic case.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please call up Prosecution Exhibit 2754.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Now that we are discussing the Stosic case, Mr. Dorovic, we will agree that case was processed to the stage it was and in your view, certain criminal offences committed by that person were covered up and you were being pressed into that by the security organs. Am I right in presenting the gist of your evidence?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: None of the matters I had been engaged in were, in fact, materialised in that case.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: I agree. And we agree that in your statement in paragraph 24 and yesterday in your evidence here, Nesic threatened you and asked that you terminate the investigation against that person?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right, and that's the first time I met Nesic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Very well. Now that I look at Prosecution Exhibit 2754, and that's the 30th of May, 1999, there you indeed mention Nesic, and that's at page 1 in both B/C/S and English versions, and you say that Nesic threatened you only in relation to the proceedings against two military officers and these are, according to my documentation, Stefanovic and Ristevski?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're right, I mention only them.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: There you don't mention Stosic?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: And we will agree that this was on the 30th of May, 1999?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as this document is concerned, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Now that we have the document, let me ask you this: You're in Pristina, you have difficulties and you're being -- or rather, pressure is being put on you and the way I read the document, you sent a threatening or a warning letter to the commander of the military district of Pristina where you say that, among other things, you will ask to be relieved of your duty unless you are given a different vehicle, a vehicle whose front door can be closed. So you're not saying in this letter that you will be resigning because of the difficulties because of the 1.040 documents that are missing; you're merely mentioning the Lada Niva 1.300 vehicle, the front door of which cannot be closed. Am I reading this right?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's the way it was written.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: I will show you a different document now, which is your statement, P2708, page 3 and page 4 in Serbian -- or rather, pages 3 and 4 in Serbian and page 5 in English. This is a document concerning the criminal proceedings instituted against you, and I will read the part concerning the problems involving Nesic. You say: "I've already explained how I was received down there in Pristina, that I -- I experienced problems from Major Nesic, who asked me to withdraw the indictment against Stefanovic and Ristevski and I had been constantly exposed to threats on this account." Mr. Dorovic, I went through the entire document and I can tell you that in this document you don't mention Stosic either.

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not even before this Tribunal from which I expect protection am I able to speak freely about Stosic; I was warned that I should not do that. May I only be given the chance to explain what I was, in fact, required to do in the Stosic case. I dare not mention Stosic beyond what I think -- I shouldn't because I was cautioned about the fact that some of Stosic's activity falls under state secret obligations, and that's why I should not tell anything more about Stosic, as I was not given the waiver by my government to do that. Now, if the Tribunal and you, Mr. Visnjic, want me to speak about that, I will go beyond that boundary in the hope that the Tribunal will protect me from the threats that were extended to me, especially in relation to Stosic. I mentioned Stosic in my statement --

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Please pause there.

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can even explain here the situations in which I was supposed to intercede for Stosic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm not following this, Mr. Dorovic. [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Your microphone, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm not following this, Mr. Dorovic. The issue at the moment is why certain documents are written in a certain way. These were written in 1999. They're nothing to do with -- at the moment with the situation today. Now, the question really is why there's no mention of Stosic in the document which you've just been shown. Then we'll deal with the other matter in a moment.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because I asked from the chief military prosecutor and his associates to be allowed to take over the case against Stosic. I wasn't allowed to do that. I was told that I should forget about all my dealings concerning the Stosic case right away. That is why I did not dare mention this before that other court and those other proceedings in Nis. However, there are written documents that I submitted to the chief military prosecutor and that I submitted to General Gojkovic upon my return from Kosovo. These documents are in possession of Colonel Nikola Petkovic, and may be made available to the Tribunal. Even though I knew that he was a member of the security service from the security administration itself, in fact, I did say that on the 6th of February, 2002, in the presence of two of his associates. I did say that openly. I suppose that these are records of my -- of my examination in the proceedings in Nis. I didn't dare mention that matter there, but I mentioned it instead to those others.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, we'll go briefly into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: So the waiver contains a number of maybe eight to 10 or 15 concrete issues that the witness is then granted permission to speak about to us and testify about to us. This witness is particularly concerned if he goes outside of these categories in any way that he may suffer consequences because of the position he is in in his system, and I think that is the cause of his concern. And there was another issue. When he came here he expected to be returning, actually, earlier than he can now. And he requested that we furnish a documentation of him being needed here because he was also afraid that he may be held responsible for being absent without granted leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, that's not the point.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: So he is just concerned about his position when he returns that he can't be attacked on any of these formalities, basically, which we consider them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But there is so much material here about Stosic. Are you telling me there's something there to restrict the extent to which he can tell us about that?

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: No, I think it only relates to the -- to the previous events previous to Kosovo because there is a long story --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That makes sense. That's got nothing to do with this case.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Yes, exactly, and maybe the witness misunderstood that he was compelled or asked about these issues. That's how I understood the confusion to have arisen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What is it you want to say, Mr. Visnjic?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, that's precisely what I wanted to ask the witness now, whether he has any restrictions on speaking about events in Kosovo in relation to Stosic or anybody else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, that was a question I had just asked him and he was in the middle of answering it by saying, "In the criminal report that was brought by the chief of the security administration it was written there that as much -- that as such he also went and worked in Kosovo. That is a criminal report containing criminal charges and is what we worked on so persistently and so seriously." Now, if you want to clarify whether there's anything in relation to that that he's prohibited from disclosing, then that's okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Dorovic, you are correct in understanding that your evidence should be confined to matters for which you have a waiver, and as far as we can tell from what the Prosecutor has said to us, there does not appear to be a restriction on the you giving evidence about Kosovo and that the areas in which there's been no waiver are areas which are irrelevant to this trial. Now, as I understand your evidence, you have very carefully tried throughout to comply with the authority you've been given to give evidence here; and as far as we can tell, absolutely nothing has happened that ought to in any way put your position in Serbia in question. And you are required to stay here as long as it is necessary for your evidence to be completed, and that's our responsibility. It's not your responsibility [Realtime transcript read in error "evidence"]. So we don't consider that anything that has occurred here should in any way prejudice your position in your job in Serbia, and we would be extremely concerned if we were to find out later that anything had happened as a result of your -- had happened in respect of your employment as a result of your presence here. Now, Mr. Visnjic, it's important --

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, may I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- that you clarify whether there are areas in relation to Kosovo that have not been dealt with -- well, it's not your -- necessarily your responsibility to do that; I quite appreciate that. But if you do wish to clarify that point, we will certainly not prevent you from doing so. Yes, Judge Kamenova's pointing out something in the transcript. Page 62, line 2, the word "evidence" is wrong there. That should be "responsibility," "it's not your responsibility." In fact, that should be corrected in the final transcript and not left to the point where we've now reached for clarification. Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if we are still in private session --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, we're not.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please move private session for a minute so I just ask the witness something, just one question. I don't want to -- I don't want to cause any danger to him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Your concern is for the witness's security or for the security of someone else?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm concerned about what he said that he has these restrictions on these answers and that's why I wanted to ask him something.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well. We shall go into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dorovic, could you please just confirm this for me. Yesterday on page 54 of the transcript, did you first mention that Stosic was linked to the Orahovac mass grave?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand. You mean here were before the Court, in the statement? No. As for his role, I spoke about that to my commander, even down there when I was prevented from working. And then I told the president of the supreme military court about this and the supreme military prosecutor and my superior and the security organs, and in writing at that. So it is recorded, like today. The 6th of February, 2002. And when I talked about Stosic, because he's their man and they're the ones who said to me that I would lose my life if ever I speak to anyone about that again.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: All right. The time is now. Did you compile an official note yourself when you spoke to the security organs and is that in the documents of this court?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One of them is. There are several of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it correct that there is an official note in the records of this court of the security organs about the interview that was conducted with you on the 6th of February, 2002, P2712, and that is the document that you, yourself, brought to this court? Am I right?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I really don't know what you're talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] P2172 [as interpreted], Your Honour, could it please be shown to the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, possibly. I don't know what it's about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now there's confusion. Is it 2712 or 2172?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] P2712.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I see this note. I didn't bring that note. This note was --

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I'm sorry. I assume not, but the Prosecutor probably showed this to you when you were preparing for your testimony here.

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I haven't studied it, but I'm aware of its existence from the work of the supreme military court, because actually it is part of the proceedings against the judges of that court that is underway now, rather, the investigation is underway against the judges who at that time were in charge of the proceedings against me. Now, they are the ones who are to be held accountable --

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. Just a moment. What was it that I asked you? What was my question?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Did I give this note, and my answer was no.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell me now, and is the name of Stosic referred to in this note?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this note? No.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Next topic: The Orahovac mass grave. Do you -- that is 3D532. Milos Spasojevic is the person who gave this statement and the KV number 106/99 that you gave is not a prosecution number but a court number. And that the documents were searched, the National Council and the Army of Serbia and Montenegro searched for these documents and they didn't find these documents.

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: KV is a lettering that is used for court cases. Anybody who ever did any work there knows that, but this is one of the 17 cases that they simply destroyed. And Stosic's is the most serious one of all of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: All right. So Stosic is more serious than the criminal report concerning Orahovac or is Stosic simultaneously the criminal report for Orahovac, the mass grave?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic, I'm going to tell you in spite of all the state secret warnings --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speakers please pause.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Where the killing takes place, that's where Stosic is. Stosic is everywhere where there is killing --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Dorovic, a very specific question has been asked. Is Stosic -- the criminal report about Orahovac, the mass grave, is that one of the reports in relation to Stosic, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In many documents out of the 150 documents of which the grave-site case consists, there are several places where Stosic and Djordjevic are mentioned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Please listen to the question. Is Stosic's involvement in Orahovac one of the 17?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Dorovic, I will also put it to you that Nedeljko Cvijovic, who was the chief of security in the military district --

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in my military district. We assumed duties on the same date.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: He also said that he wasn't aware of a mass grave in the Orahovac area. Mr. Dorovic, do you allow for the possibility that this mass grave at Orahovac, as you refer to it, you mistook for a different mass grave that was the subject of criminal investigation?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic, this is the second time you're offending me.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry if I offended you. So the answer is no?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't rule out -- I rule out that possibility. I worked on that case, and, Mr. Visnjic, one does not forget these matters. This was one of the stolen cases and Cvijovic himself who stole that case.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Very well. We will take it one step at a time and we will get to those stolen files.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic, are you tell us which mass grave it was mistaken for, because then you might get an answer that means something?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, that's the mass grave mentioned as Pusto Selo or Senovac in the documents. I do believe there will be more discussion of that later on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What is your point, that there's no mass grave at Orahovac?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'm trying to ask the witness if it's true that an investigation was carried out into a mass grave but that it was, in fact, the one at Pusto Selo or Senovac. The witness, however, keeps insisting that it's quite a different location.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, you should have put that specific question.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Dorovic, in paragraph 32 of your statement you said that when you came to Kosovo, before that, your deputy Djuro Blagojevic returned 1.040 criminal reports to the people who filed them. Yesterday in your evidence you mentioned again that the figure of 1.040 missing case files --

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: -- yes, reports, I apologise -- was in fact a way to cover up certain criminal offences, including, as I understand, some criminal offences against the civilian population, looting, and so on and so forth. Is my understanding correct?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I, in fact, said that my superiors were convinced that way since they sent me over there, because the meeting that they held in early May, General Gojovic spoke about 1.040 missing criminal reports and he said that this omission on their part could not be rectified. In my view, most of them had to do with the army, with the failure to respond to call-ups and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: As you arrived in Kosovo - this is something you learned from Gojovic in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, from Gojovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: As you arrived in Kosovo, were you able to satisfy yourself directly about the situation?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we -- I could not, Mr. Visnjic. We did not have the register or anything of that sort.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Very well. Let me show you Exhibit 3D533, page 5 in Serbian and page 5 in English. Mr. Dorovic, let me tell you that this is a report on crime between 23 March and 1st May, 1999, sent by the military prosecutor from the Pristina Military District, your predecessor, Djura Blagojevic.

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that. I don't see the signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: I will show it to you right now.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the usher give the witness this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: While you're looking at the document, Mr. Dorovic, I will read a portion of it out loud. This is the section which says that it was -- what characterises the crimes of failure to respond to a call-up, an invasion of military service under Article 214, that after the first 40 reports were filed with the prosecutor's office by the Pristina Military District command, the military prosecutor asked for 40 investigations to be initiated, 36 were completed, and the military prosecutor dropped the prosecutions against the 36 persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think there was an error, page 70, line 14 [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Then the document reads -- not you, sorry.

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, I have nothing to do with this. I see this for the first time.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: I apologise. The document reads: "For all these reasons, all the criminal reports submitted later on by the district were not processed, but the prosecutor asked for additional check-ups with the person who filed the criminal report, and such action taken by the prosecutor is probably the main reason why the military district command did not continue submitting such reports."

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not get your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: I will just put it to you. Does this tally with the missing reports that Mr. Gojovic told you of?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understood it this way. Perhaps it's the interpretation. This is about just 40 reports, and there were 1.040 reports missing. This is April. We're talking about March and we're talking about the beginning of the war and about 1.040 criminal reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Are you quite positive about that figure?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's more documents than this, it's more documents than this. Those were hundreds of official documents --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Let's take this in stages so we are helped by the document. Do you recognise the signature on the screen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, really, no. Djuro Blagojevic was one of my deputies. He was my predecessor. I don't know if this is his signature. He was one of my deputies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Let's go to the part that Mr. Visnjic has been referring to so we can read it, because what he's read indicates no reason for these proceedings being dropped and may not be inconsistent with your evidence. Not that page, we want -- sorry. Now, do you read the explanation there, the part that's underlined, and tell us if you think this relates to the 1.040, that because something went wrong with the first 36 they decided not to bother with the others.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For God's sake, this refers to 40 reports. All of us in the army knew about the others. 1.040? That's quite a different figure. This is something different. At the meeting in Belgrade an example was raised to show the then-prosecutor Djuro Blagojevic's omissions at work. He was working in Pristina. They were unable to find these reports. They simply vanished in the air, and this was something that the military judiciary was aware of. You can find that in the reports, or rather, in the information that General Gojovic provided where he spoke of the functioning of the military judiciary early on at the beginning of the war and he speaks about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I don't know if you've really addressed the question because it says that the military prosecutor asked for 40 investigations to be initiated, 36 were completed, and he then dropped the prosecutions against the 36. And the document goes on to say: "For all these reasons the criminal reports submitted later on by the district were not processed, but the prosecutor asked for additional check-ups with the person who filed the criminal report. And such action taken by the prosecutor is probably the main reason why the military district didn't continue to submit the reports." So what they're saying is that there was a failure to submit reports, and you say that over a thousand were submitted and then returned. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They vanished without trace. One doesn't know whether they were returned to those who filed them in the first place. We don't even know who delivered them. We know that there were 1.040 reports. The prosecutors from the military district said that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That answers my question. Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I don't want to comment on this any further. I think -- I believe the text is self-explanatory.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dorovic, yesterday in your evidence you said that among these reports there were reports concerning crimes against the civilian population. Is that your evidence still today?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never said that they were among the 1.040. It is probable that there were some. The fact of the matter is that we had such cases among that group of 17 case files.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Let's leave those 17 case files aside for now.

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that there were some and that they vanished. What they contained is improper of us to speculate upon.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: I'm merely quoting your words from yesterday's transcript.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Can we have reference for that, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Transcript page 99, line -- lines 15 to 21. Should I quote?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, please continue with the next question. We've got to make more rapid progress than this, Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we will be going through this quickly. 3D534 should be called up, page 1 specifically.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dorovic, I will read to you the information on the activity ever since its setting up on the 31st of May, 1999. This is a report by the military prosecutor to the Pristina Military District command. Page 1, paragraph 3 reads: "On this occasion we wish to" -- "let us remind you once again that instead of entering the first 492 criminal reports filed against non-serving civilians who are liable for military service for the crime of failure to respond," and so on and so forth, "because it was more than clear from the content of the reports that no crimes had been committed, which is why probably no evidence was provided with the reports." Is it true that there were merely 492 criminal reports, Mr. Dorovic?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean that those that were dismissed -- returned? No, 492 are those that are contained in the register. I believe I drafted this report. I should be the signatory.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: We will read the second paragraph of this item where -- which reads: "It soon turned out that this was the right decision" --

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: " -- because in the legal procedure for acquiring information from those who filed the criminal reports and as a result of the requests sent three times to the Pristina Military District command it was established beyond doubt that the reported individuals had responded to the call-up in time and reported to RJ, which means that the criminal offences cited in the reports or any other criminal offences subject to prosecution ex officio had not been committed and that even if such obviously groundless criminal reports were by any chance to be considered as criminal reports, then they should equally be considered dismissed in due process by a single decision jointly applicable to all of these reports."

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and every single one of them was registered and dismissed, and you can read them, Mr. Visnjic. This is quite something different. It does not refer to the vanished --

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wrote this.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: That's why we are going to read the next passage that refers to that situation and it says in here: "The regularity of this decision is confirmed by the fact that in 40 cases in which investigation was requested and conducted on the basis of such evidently baseless reports, the military prosecutor had no other option but to cease prosecution because the results of the investigation confirmed that there is no crime that may be prosecuted ex officio." Mr. Dorovic, I put it to you that in this document what is described is the situation that was described in the previous document signed by Blagojevic and, in the situation that happened the way it did, there is nothing that would point to the fact that something was being concealed and that was within the jurisdiction of this court.

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a totally erroneous conclusion on your part, groundless, and I should only be happy if that was the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dorovic, could you please read -- first of all, tell me, when did the 1.040 reports go missing?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I already told you at the beginning of the war. If I have to pin-point it in time, it was sometime before the mid-April of that year.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you read the title of this document.

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know the title of this document. It is: "Information of work up to 31 May."

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Can you read the whole title.

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Supreme military prosecutor" --

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Can you go on reading?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Information on the work up to 31 May 1999."

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: When was the military prosecutor's office established?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't talk about the Pristina district, but I believe that it was on the 24th and started operating on the 26th.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Dorovic. And finally --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, can I just be clear on one thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You said this was your document.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But the reference here is the office at the 3rd Army command. Is that the office you were in? I understood that you were the command of the Pristina Military District.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, there is a stamp of the addressee on the left-hand side, and it shows you who were the -- where the document originated from.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the left upper corner.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Maybe you can't see it but you can see it now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the left upper corner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is that where the document is being sent to though? No?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the right-hand side is the addressee and, on the left, where it comes from.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. That's where it comes from. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: In the transcript you said that the prosecution started -- was founded on the 24th and it became operational on the 26th of March, 1999. Is that so?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that I was not sure, that I assumed that this was the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: And this information is relative to the work from the foundation to the 31st of May. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: If we turn this document to the last page, am I right in saying that if you signed the document, Mr. Dorovic, that this is the case.

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't see the signature, but yes, I did. I know that I drafted this information.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Can you look at the document in the Serbian language.

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, this is my signature, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have more questions. Mr. Dorovic, we are moving to the disappearance of 17 files that went missing from the court in Pristina, apparently. These are paragraphs 27, 37, and 38 of your statement, and according to you, these were files speaking on the expulsion of Catholic Albanians from Glavicica on Christmas Eve, Rugova, destruction of Albanian houses near Pec, and some other files that you mentioned already.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dorovic, you had already informed different bodies about these cases. You informed the army, the court, maybe even the general public. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you are. From 1999 onwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Yes, we agree on that. In a letter Exhibit Number P2730, this is a letter that you wrote to Svetko Kovac. You say in this letter that -- and he at the time was the chief of security of the Federal Ministry of Defence, I suppose. You say in this letter that -- in the last paragraph, that is, you say that as a military prosecutor, you had been stolen 17 case files and destroyed evidence on crimes for unlawful expropriation of valuable Siptar cars. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: And you also say that none of the crimes that I have just spoken about, the expulsion of Albanian Catholics, the burning down of -- villages, the destruction of houses in Istok, Pec, Orahovac, Stosic, and so on and so forth. We have spoken about Stosic and said why but not about others?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But this is from June and I provided him with written documents on the 6th of February in front of his man. We had been there all day. They filed 11 criminal reports. Colonel Kovac himself will tell you that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: He will tell me, as he did in Exhibit 272 [as interpreted], the official note where he says that on page 2, item 5, you list a certain number of omissions and transgressions and you say that unlawfully, property was taken from Siptars and he says that in the prosecutor's office in Pristina there is evidence of 17 cases of fictitious confiscation of vehicles. Again in this document dated 6th February 2001 and 10 May 2001 there is no mention of all these cases relative to other crimes, save for the problems with the confiscation of property and vehicles from Albanians.

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic, you should ask Kovac why he omitted to record my words that I spoke to him. Although I speak very fast, I had to be slowed down. I provided him with concrete evidence primarily for the 11 of his men were -- and the first one of them is Mr. Stosic --

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dorovic, I'm not interested in people, I'm interested in crimes and we agree that there is nothing about them in the document?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know. You have to ask him. I can't draw such a conclusion. I am not familiar with the document, first of all. I've already told you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: That document was before you a minute ago.

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You've never provided me with this document. I don't know whose document this is.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the usher please provide the witness with the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, the document is on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Oh, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It can be read on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this is the previous document and after that I called up 2712 of June 2001. P2712 is the document that I'm referring to. Second page, item 5 in the Serbian language, the same thing in English, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Why don't we read other parts? Why isn't there anything else mentioned in here? I've spoken about a hundred of things and more specifically about 11 --

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dorovic, in this document do you see anywhere that any other crime is mentioned for which you claimed in your statement that they can be found in the 17 files, save for the document speaking about the confiscation of vehicles and property?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please allow me to read. I can't speak about the document without reading. I need time. I can't talk off my head.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: I agree with you. While you're looking at the document and then you will answer questions about it?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I please ask the usher to provide the witness with a document.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Let me remind you while you're looking at the document, let me remind you of another exhibit; 2781 is the number of that exhibit. We don't have to call it up on the screen. The Judges have it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: One at a time.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: I agree.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've spoken at length about Colonel Milan Karan and Aleksandar Papac who attended the conversation, asked me to stop working on the Stosic case. That is one reason why they were not mentioned and that is also a reason why they made me go and write the article, because I was afraid they would kill me that day. They forebade me to do anything. I'm talking about Nesic here. I explained to them in great length, so it is mentioned here. You're not right, Mr. Visnjic, when you say that there is nothing. In the Serbian version you will see it on the first paragraph on page 3, here you can see it nicely that this is mentioned. This is what they wrote. This is a representation of this conversation, a very unprofessional, very improper representation. The fact is that the two of them personally, Colonel Papac, Aleksander Papac --

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Let's not go that way. I asked you whether in this document any other crimes are mentioned against the civilian Albanian population save for the confiscation of property and vehicles. That is my question to you.

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they are mentioned and this is exactly what I am talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Can you please read it? Can you please read it?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He pointed out that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Plesae stop. It's on page 3, apparently, of the Serbian. Which page in the English is it in? And let's have on the screen what it is we are about to be told about. So the last part of the document in English as well, please. Now, what is it you want to explain, Mr. Dorovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, at the time I explained at great length everything about Stosic, although they knew more than I did because they were the ones who sent him there to do what he did. Those who were present there on the day asked me to stop working on that case, to stop talking about the case, to go into retirement --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We have all that. What you're going to point out to us is where something along these lines is mentioned in this document. You've just told us it's there on page 3, so where is it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the first paragraph he pointed out that a certain Major Nesic from the security body of the command of the military district in Pristina put pressure on him to give up on prosecution of several persons --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter cannot follow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Please slow down. The interpreter can't follow you. Continue reading more slowly, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Put pressure on him to give up on the prosecution of several cases for which criminal reports were filed by the security organ of the Pristina Corps. Allegedly, there are documents to that effect in the military prosecutor's office of the Pristina Corps, not allegedly. There are, in fact, such documents in the case where a decision was brought by the court, a collective decision --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You've pointed out where it is in the document. Mr. Visnjic, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, can the witness please be shown Exhibit 2781. This is a criminal report that the witness issued against unknown judges and unknown persons for 17 crimes contained in several case files. And I would kindly ask the witness to be shown page 1, paragraph 1 of that document, where it says that the persons reported in relation to 17 criminal cases of the military court of Pristina Military District command, that is, from 15 case files -- cases in relation to investigation requests and two cases as per indictments brought by the military prosecutor before that court during the state of war illegally take and hide a number of documents, documentation, certificates, and temporarily confiscated items, vehicles, driving licences, and traffic licences for those vehicles, official notes of authorised officials of the VJ security organ, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dorovic, in your document in your criminal report that you filed against 17 individuals -- actually, against unknown individuals, you still went on to mention only documents relative to vehicles, the vehicles confiscated from Albanians.

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not only that documentation. I don't mention only that. In the explanation of the decision I speak about other things as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Are you referring to the explanation of the criminal report?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, criminal report.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Let's stop here. Page 2, paragraph 4, please, at the explanation of the criminal report. Among the case files that were returned, there were also 17 case files in which -- from which the individuals reported concealed documents Ristevski and Stefanovic are two against whom prosecution had started. In the English that is also page 2, paragraph 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can you scroll down a little in the English. The Serbian version is okay, but we need to scroll down in the English and go to the next page, please, in the English version to display the text. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: This is a long amount -- but it says here: "Among the returned documents there are also two cases against Ristevski and Stefanovic as well as the 15 cases pertaining to requests for the investigation of members of those organs and their associates from which the persons reported had stolen and hidden certificates on temporarily confiscated items. 10 expensive passenger vehicles taken from Siptar civilians as well as statements of the accused, witness statements," and so on and so forth. Mr. Dorovic, again you don't mention any other crime that you mention in your statement as being in the case files of these cases from which parts of the documentation went missing. Am I right in saying this?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're partly right, Mr. Visnjic. What you have just quoted refers to two indictments that were issued in my office, and we are talking about the investigations that were carried out by the court of the Pristina Corps which pronounced itself incompetent and wanted us to act because they thought that we were competent for those cases. In those cases, as a matter of fact, in all the 15 cases there are those serious crimes, among them the mass grave that I was talking about and the other cases that you have just listed. And why am I not mentioning them here?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: But this is not in the 15 case files for which you filed criminal reports.

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, these are those cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: But you don't mention those crimes?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already told you, I did not dare as mention Stosic and others --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I thought the 17 were cases where the files disappeared. And here we're talking about 17 cases where the files are returned. So how do these relate to each other?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the way I understood it is that from the 17 case files -- first of all, the witness stated that 17 17 case files were stolen but we have it here that documents were stolen from the 17 case files but the case files still exist. This is what I understood from the report. But we have the witness here. Maybe he could explain.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] These are cases that were under investigation and some of them, I believe at least three of them, were issued against requests for some investigative procedures that were to be taken by the investigative judge of the military court with the command of the Pristina Corps. These investigative judges were in a very dire straits --

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Let's not go into all the teats, Mr. Dorovic; it's very simple.

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not simple at all. It is by no means simple at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Some things are simpler than you would like to make them, I suspect. In paragraph 17 of your statement you say: "They stole the files of the 17 cases from the office of the court in Pristina." And this document says: "The Pristina Military District command returned to the military prosecutor at the said command a number of documents pertaining to the criminal cases of previously initiated investigation reports. Among the returned documents, there were also 17 case files from which the said persons had stolen and hidden material evidence on the crimes committed." Now, are these the 17 -- the same 17 cases?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, they're the same, or rather, 15 of them; if we take into account the indictments, the indictments are separate. However, this has to do with the investigation stage. These are cases --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Stop. Just deal with my -- I'm -- I'm obviously not as quick and bright as you are; it takes me a little time to take in the details of things like this. And you've also the advantage of having been involved when we were not involved. So please answer the questions. 17 -- what are the two that are not part of the 17?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ristevski and Stefanovic, because those indictments were issued by my office of the prosecutor, the first VTK 390 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just stop there. I am having difficulty with -- in understanding. 17 files were stolen, and papers from 17 files were returned. These are the two things we've got. Now, are they not the same 17 files in both cases?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] These were court files from the Pristina court, whereas I am talking about part of the documents, the files, the prosecution files that went missing first. And then every trace was lost of all files, everything was lost, including those two; all 17, that is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just stop there. If they are files -- 17 from the prosecutor and 17 from the court, do they relate to the same 17 cases?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 15 are the same ones, so there are two indictments that were issued in this prosecution office and these 15 cases are the cases that we're talking about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So in two cases nothing was returned; is that the position?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Everything went missing, everything. Ultimately, they took everything in the evening on the 30th. I personally reported Lieutenant-Colonel Cvijevic as the person responsible and Nesic, too, and there are other reports in which I was actually more specific, the one that I submitted to the security organs with the permission of the supreme military prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, perhaps the parties in their questions will manage to clarify this. I certainly am baffled. I make that clear to you at the moment, about the other -- the two that seem to be separate from the others. Now, Mr. Visnjic, I think you've probably had as much time as we can possibly allow you --

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour -- Your Honour, I will have perhaps another ten minutes of questions for this witness, if you allow me to do so. You see that I am struggling with time all the time but ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah, I recognise that, but the same happened yesterday with the Prosecution. You're both suffering from the same difficulty, which is not of your -- well, not entirely of your own making.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just one more thing, Your Honour. Correction in the transcript while we can still see it. The witness refers to the name of Lieutenant-Colonel Cvijevic in several documents. It is actually Nedeljko Cvijovic. Let us not have any problems later in terms of identifying this person, this Nedeljko Cvijovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Nedeljko.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: It is 3D543.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, you're right. We started together down there, Nedeljko Cvijovic, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just one final question, Mr. Dorovic, if -- are you saying that this document on the screen now must be wrong because nothing was ever returned to your office?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was stolen, Mr. President. They seized it, they stole it, on the evening of the 31st of May. All the documents --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Would you listen to my question. Are you saying this document here must be wrong when it says: "Among the returned documents there were also 17 case files ..."?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I am talking about the exchange of cases between the Pristina Corps and the military district. I, as prosecutor, was attached to the Pristina district, whereas these 15 cases were cases that were dealt with by the investigative judge of the other district court attached to the Pristina Corps. So when I say "returned," I'm referring to the return of those documents and files allegedly to that court because that court had claimed that they had no jurisdiction allegedly, and then they ordered that nevertheless these cases should be dealt with by the military prosecutor and then that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Stop, stop, stop, please. Ms. Moeller, can you explain this to me?

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Your Honour, what the witness just said is what is also in paragraph 27 of his statement. This return was -- he was asked to return cases that had -- that he had taken on from the military prosecutor at the command back to this command because it was said he didn't have jurisdiction and that's the first sentence in paragraph 27. "They were turned over from Spasojevic from me" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: To Spasojevic, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Yeah, to, and Spasojevic was -- the witness was at the military district court and Spasojevic was at the military prosecutor at the command; so that was the turning back and forth of the cases that he talked to. And maybe the confusion comes from there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But these -- this talks about them coming back where?

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Back to Spasojevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I can't read the top. Somebody's magnified it. Can we see the top of this document as well -- let's just see the whole page.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: It's on the English version on page 3, the top paragraph says: "The military court at Pristina Military District command," which -- "and returned to the military prosecutor at said command a number of documents."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: "Pertaining to criminal cases."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So these are being sent from Mr. Dorovic --

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: They are from the military district --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- because he's at the military district of Pristina, so he's sending them.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: He's sending them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That doesn't explain this. It says that he's sending 17 case files from which people had stolen and hidden material evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: No. He was ordered to return these cases to the prosecutor at the military command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And I understood that was because the claim was that he had no jurisdiction over these cases.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: So he had to return them to the military command to Mr. Spasojevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, but when that happened, there were already documents stolen from them, according to --

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: No, that's not my understanding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No. Read what it says: "Among the returned documents there were also 17 case files from which the said persons had stolen and hidden material evidence." So that has happened before they're returned, unless the translation's wrong.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: That -- yes. I understand that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm totally baffled by this.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: -- may be the translation then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And we will look into that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We need a break now, Mr. Dorovic, for lunch. The usher will show you again where to go.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And we'll resume at five minutes to 2.00. --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.53 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We need a break now, Mr. Dorovic, for lunch. The usher will show you again where to go.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And we'll resume at five minutes to 2.00. --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.53 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Dorovic, in your statement you spoke about certain disciplinary measures that were taken against you, and my question to you is very specific. Is it true that at the time the federal minister for defence, General Dragoljub Ojdanic, did not want to sign the proposed decision on you being prosecuted by the military court? Is that the case?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I learned from a person --

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Is it true or not?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was told that this is the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Can this be found in the documents that were sent to you from the Ministry of Defence in response to some of your requests? Am I right?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In different and very odd context when I wanted all this to be put to an end but they've never wanted to do that --

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: I agree with you. But the fact is am I right?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please. Mr. Visnjic, in the documents that arrived from his office pursuant to the order of the court when I wanted the court to put the proceedings to an end, either to convict me or to find me not guilty, then my administration told me that General Ojdanic had not accepted the request but he never issued a formal decision, either.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: I agree with you. Thank you. And then yesterday in paragraphs 40 to 46 of your statement you spoke about the meetings dealing with certain problems concerning vehicles which were in the possession of the Army of Yugoslavia. And as far as I understand your statement, you say that the General Staff put pressure on Gojovic and Obrencevic --

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: And that they conveyed that to you. So nobody actually put pressure on you. The pressure was put on the two of them?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, on both me and Dr. Grigorije Spasojevic in the segment of our work when we were issued the task to prepare a draft of the decision to be signed by the Chief of General Staff and following at the end was to send this to the Ministry of Defence to sign. It was said that the vehicles will never be returned by the General Staff, that they wanted to keep them. General Uzelac conveyed this to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: It was conveyed to you, the two of you by General Uzelac?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
