utterances.text: And to the working group and to me and to Grigorije Spasojevic, because the two of us remained to draft this as well, I remained, I stayed behind to sign this letter.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'm going to refer you to the statement 3D539 which is the statement by Svetozar Obrencevic and 3D538, the statement by Milos Gojkovic, and I will not belabour on that point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Before you move on. Mr. Dorovic, at the end of your last answer you said that the two of us remained to draft this letter as well, I remained, I stayed behind to sign this letter. Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To prepare a draft for the letter to the signed by the Chief of the General Staff. The draft of the decision exists. It was the Chief of the General Staff who was supposed to sign the letter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's all I wanted to be clear about. Thank you. Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dorovic, can the two of us agree -- or let me approach it in a different way. The OTP has disclosed to us some of the requests for your dismissal -- 2775 P and 2777 are the numbers of the documents -- actually, 2778, the request that you, or the notice letters that you have submitted in the course of your career. Am I right when I say that in none of these documents there is a reason which you state in the statement that the security organs tried to get involved in your work?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're not right. This is probably a conclusion that you drew from the analysis of these requests. You will see in my request and in the decision to be conveyed, which was supposed to be arrived at the minister's desk in order to be conveyed to the president and no reasons are mentioned and it is not by chance that the supreme military prosecutor wrote and in the president's decision it says on request. And one more thing. I did not request that only on two occasions. I requested for my dismissal on four occasions. I have seen three of them here, and the fourth one is missing.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: I apologise. I have only two of your requests. One dated the 18th of January, 1997, and the other 30 March 1998.

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And there is another one that you've just analysed, and the fourth one is missing, and in that one after having worked with Tijanic and with two cases, I wanted to be relieved of my duties as a prosecutor. They had decided that I should go to Kosovo, and they explained to me that I am needed over there.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Am I right in saying that you, while you were the deputy prosecutor --

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And, Your Honours, I'm referring you to the statement 3D --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: If the counsel could repeat the numbers which the interpreters failed to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can you repeat the numbers, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 3D539 and 3D538.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: On several occasions you got into a conflict with the parties, the judges, the attorneys at law, and sometimes you would even abandon the hearing or the judges would abandon the hearing and they asked Colonel Petkovic to intervene.

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're talking about a very specific case that is notorious not only in the army but in Serbia as a whole. This is the case when I attended a trial for a whole day, and then I lerned learned that the decision had already been written. It's a notorious case. The judge had already drafted the decision in an ample number of copies and he decided that the person would be released from prison. He took 7.800 Deutschemarks for that. The president of the court knew it, the prosecutor knew, everybody knew about that. When I learned about that, I filed a criminal report against that judge and I left the courtroom. I can only tell you that I went on foot to my house, and I'm talking about a distance of more than 6 kilometres. I was angry, I was cross, I was outraged. My bosses understood that, and they know what the real reason was. That was the real reason. I have never come into conflict with anybody before or after. I can only tell you that I was fortunate -- or misfortunate that I was dealing with the most difficult cases, and this is what Mr. Nikola Petkovic, Colonel Nikola Petkovic pointed out in my assessment. It is not true that I was in conflict with everybody. I was in conflict with one judge and with the president of the court, Gojovic, who wanted to cover this up. Everybody else was afraid and they said if the general public learned about that, that the military prosecutor's office and the judiciary would stop existing. And then I said it should not have been set up in the first place if the cases are fabricated and rigged and such a judiciary system should not exist. And this is the truth, Mr. Visnjic, and this is my bosses -- this is what my boss is going to tell you. I believe that Petkovic is going to confirm this. There is a criminal report. There is a decision by the Supreme Military Court in that case, and you can verify all this, and if there is any difference in my bosses, they will confirm this. If the Trial Chamber wants me, I can consult my notebook and I can give you the numbers of the court, the number of the prosecutor's office for this file, and if you want to verify any of this, I believe that you will find out all that. It is a notorious case. A lot of people know about it. I believe this is the case that you are talking about and the traces of that file still -- and the case still exists in the court. On four occasions I asked it be dismissed --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... yet again to bring some sort of reality to you, Mr. Dorovic. We do not have forever in this court to listen to endless explanations when there is a simple answer to the question, which you have already given. Please allow us to make progress with the case; otherwise, we will not hear the important parts of the evidence that you can give to us. This is obviously something you feel passionate about because of the way it affected you personally but -- and I sympathise with that. But there are much bigger and broader issues to be addressed by you here. So please bring some perspective to bear on the way in which you answer questions. Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have spent my ten minutes and all of my questions for this witness. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Visnjic. Mr. Aleksic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, sir. My learned friend Visnjic has asked you a lot of questions, but I have a few things that I would like to discuss with you. At the beginning of the sitting today you said that you spent some eight days in Kosovo all together.

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Up to the moment when I wrote the report on the 31st. On the 4th of June I was in custody all day. In the evening I was taken to Nis, and from there I was sent to Belgrade. So I was returned from Kosovo on the 4th in the evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: But your request for dissolution was submitted on the 30th?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, after Stosic's attack and after I had learned that my case files had been stolen and after the decision of the collegium on the advice of the supreme military prosecutor that I should draft a note on all that, that it should be done in a very formal way.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: I apologise for interrupting you. We will come to that day. Now something that you told us yesterday in the transcript, this is on page 37 to 40, you spoke about a document that was mentioned in your analysis, and this analysis is an exhibit before this Chamber, speaking about the work of the military courts. And you also spoke about the application of the international rule of war in the armed forces of Yugoslavia, and this was issued sometime on the 10th of June, 1998 [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I spoke about two documents. One of them was issued in 1991. This is an order of the minister of defence and an instruction of the minister of defence on --

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: The instruction --

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But you mentioned the year 1988, so I suppose that you are talking about the instruction on how to apply the international rules of law.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Yes, this is what I said. You should listen to me.

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I'm listening, but I was talking about two orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Yes, this is the instruction on applying the international rules of law in the armed forces of the SFRY of the 10th of June 1988. Do you understand?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I'm now clear on what you're talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: On page 40, line 14 to 22, in response to my learned friend Moeller's question, who asked you whether this instruction prescribes any measures or a minimum penalty, you said that no minimum or maximum penalty or any penalty whatsoever are prescribed in this particular document or instruction, to be more specific. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is what I said, this is what I think. This is a very voluminous instruction.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Am I right in saying that one of the basic obligatory elements of a crime for a crime to exist is that a penalty is prescribed for such a crime, both a minimum and a maximum.

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Am I right in saying that only a law, a republican or a federal or a general or a special law, can prescribe whether a certain behaviour represents a crime?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely, in our system.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Yes, this is the system that I'm talking about, our system. Now, let's go back to the document that we have discussed, that we have spoken about.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You have told us how you came up with your analysis and you said that this document, the instruction on applying the rules of the international rules of war in the armed forces of Yugoslavia dated the 10th of June, 1988, was signed by the then-defence secretary of the SFRY who --

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was Nikola Ljubicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Yes. Am I right in saying that the federal secretary for defence is a member of the general government or the executive power?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely, you're right, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Dorovic. Am I right in saying that a document issued by the executive power, such as this instruction, cannot be used to prescribe something that has to be prescribed by law, for example, a crime?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now I understand you. I believe that you have taken a wrong way in Article 21 of the instruction --

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: No, no, we'll come to that. I'm going to ask you that.

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're not right. If you want a yes or no answer, then the answer is no, you're not right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Article 21 speaks about the responsibility, not about criminal responsibility; am I right in saying that?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Article 21 reminds the officers --

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you whether this is about responsibility or criminal responsibility.

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I should have to look at it. If my memory serves me right, I even quoted that article --

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: That's no problem at all. We will call up the document on e-court?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The number is --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The responsibility is also a subtitle --

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Hold on just a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is P2672, the last page in both versions, the last paragraph on that page, where this Article 21 of the instructions is quoted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm addressing both Mr. Aleksic and Mr. Dorovic. You will need to slow down and observe some break or pause between the question and the answer so that the interpreters can catch up. Otherwise, we will lose some of this important evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Your Honours, and I apologise to the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I also apologise. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dorovic, have you got this Article 21 before you?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Is there a word here "criminal"?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is implied, sir. It's not written there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: It is not there but it is implied. I have no further questions about this topic. I would like to move on to your statement. As far as your statement is concerned, I would like to know this about your career. I'm not clear on one thing. This is paragraph 2. You said that you graduated from the faculty of law in Pristina, and then towards the end you say, I worked in the civil municipal court in Berane" and then you returned. Can you explain how this came about?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Gladly. According to the internship programme - and I'm sure that you're familiar with that - in the military there is a one-month period or a 30-day period during which a future military lawyers have to be familiarised with the work of the civilian courts. In the month of May 1881 [as interpreted] spent a month in a civilian court --

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: This is not clear in your statement, but now I am clear and I have no further questions on that. I shall move on. Paragraph 4 of your statement says that you were appointed as the military prosecutor in Belgrade and then in Pristina on the 20th of May. Can you please tell us -- and you also told us that military courts and prosecutor offices were set up at the beginning of the war. As far as Belgrade and the 1st Army are concerned, can you tell us how many prosecutor's offices were set up? First Belgrade, then Pristina.

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Belgrade there were --

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: I'm asking about first-instance courts.

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was one with the command of the Belgrade corps, it was either the second or the first, as you well; and then with the command of the air force and then the command of the anti-air force forces -- anti-aircraft forces --

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: So if I understand you well, there were five courts and first-instance prosecutor's office in the 1st Army?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Since you have told my colleague Visnjic that your not sure pursuant to which order the courts were established in the 3rd Army, I would kindly ask Exhibit Number 45153 [as interpreted] to be placed on e-court. This is an order of the command of the 3rd Army, 4 P 153 [as interpreted]. This was signed by the Chief of General Staff, General-Major Ljubisa Stanimirovic. The date is 28 March 1999. Do you agree -- first look at it if you need to look at it. Do you agree with me that this decision served to establish five first-instance prosecutor's offices and courts and the second-instance prosecutor's office that -- a department, a detached department of the prosecutor's office with the command of the 3rd Army? Am I right?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I personally think that you are absolutely wrong, that you are very much mistaken. All courts and military prosecutor's offices had existed before the war. On the 24th of March, when the decision of the government was proclaimed, you know that it was proclaimed at 8.00 in the evening, and automatically by a law without any additional documents or orders, military courts and prosecutor's offices had to become functioning. This is my position. And truth be told, I really don't know what you're asked me about this document. I don't understand your question. Are you asking me to count the prosecutor's offices and courts? I can do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: You didn't allow me to finish. I just wanted to ask you this: Do you agree with me that in the course of the war there were five first-instance courts and five first-instance prosecutor's offices in the zone of responsibility of the 3rd Army? That was my question.

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again I would have to count them. Believe me --

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: You can read the document; that's why I'm showing it to you.

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the 2nd Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: No. In the 3rd Army, item 2, prosecutor's offices --

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm confused about the 2nd and the 3rd Armies. There are a lot of reasons for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: But don't go into that.

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first-instance institutions they are here --

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Do you agree with me that there are five first-instance prosecutor's offices?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You have already spoken about my next topic with my colleague Visnjic. It is not disputable that you left on the 22nd, but how did that transpire? Why were you sent there? In paragraph 9 of your statement you say: "On 19 May," and you confirmed yesterday that the statement is truthful, that it corresponds to the truth and that you would repeat it to the letter. You say in your statement: "On the 19th of May I wrote a request to be relieved of duty to the supreme military prosecutor because of pressures and threats," and I won't go into any details of those. And then -- just a moment, please. Bear with me. In paragraph 21 you say again about those threats -- I apologise. And by an order of President Milosevic you were appointed on the 15th of May, according to you, and there is nothing contestable about that. This is Exhibit Number 2780, a prosecutor's exhibit. Just bear with me for another moment. And then earlier today in answering my colleague Visnjic's questions on page 69/2, you said that in practical terms, the decision by the supreme prosecutor to be sent to Kosovo was issued at the beginning of May. Now can you tell me of these dates, which one is correct? Was it at your request? Was it punishment? Or was it reward? Because there are four different documents with four different pieces of information.

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you read my official war assessment --

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: We'll come to that.

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But it says in those documents --

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: But you said --

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But it says in my assessment what was the reason for me being sent to Kosovo. It says that I sent -- I went at my own request. You have to know that I had asked for that. On the 19th I requested that, but this was my third request as a war prosecutor --

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Can I stop you there. Very well then. So this is the truth. It is the truth what you said. But then what you said in the statement, that you were transferred because of a conflict and because you did not want to obey your superior's orders, then that's not true. What is true of the two things?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Mr. Aleksic. I wanted to be dissolved of my duties because I could not bear the pressure and torture by the security organs. I wanted to be protected. I asked for protection from General Obrencevic. First he promised me and then he decided to accept my request and now if you're talking about a reward or a punishment you have to call them. According to my official assessment, this is a decision according to which I was useful if I was sent over there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: We'll come to that. And now with my colleague Visnjic you discussed the topic of Tijanic and proceedings against him. I have to ask you some other things, and I will try not to repeat anything that has already been said. In paragraph 17 of your statement you say this: "Pavkovic and Lazarevic gave us Tijanic reserve officers in the technical procurement department in the Pristina Corps authority to collect goods in the form of material goods, clothing, cigarettes, coffee, and everything else that might be of use to the Pristina Corps." And you proceed to say: "Tijanic and other witnesses in their written statements stated that Tijanic carried out all these operations on the orders of Pavkovic and Lazarevic." This is what you said. Can you please tell us as you sit today which witnesses provided statements and stated this. Can you give me any names, please?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, these were persons who provided written statements to the security organs. I will tell you that over there there is a statement by Buba Morina about her material being given to them --

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: I'm not talking about that. I'm asking you for the name of a witness who spoke about Tijanic working on the order of Pavkovic and Lazarevic?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Buba had written it down. There are written statements to that effect and I am saying to you that at least 30 people in very high positions and even the highest position, if I may say, from my point of view, from my aspect, and there are also --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Dorovic, names, please, that's what you're being asked for. Just deal with the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kertes, Mihalj Kertes, the chief of the customs administration.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's in your statement already. It's other names that Mr. Aleksic is asking about, other witnesses who give written statements. Can you give us some names or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can, Mr. President, Your Honours, but just bear with me. Who among the top personnel from the state administration was that. First of all, I can't remember the name. Bojic is the family name, and I don't know what his position was, Dr. Bojic, the minister for health. Furthermore, the director of Belgradja Denka [phoen] department store, whose name I don't know. Furthermore, the directors of Naftagas, Ina, the company from Rakovica for processing oil derivatives. In other words, the top executives who had confirmed that they had given assistance to the armed forces and it was collected by Tijanic on the order of General Ojdanic and Pavkovic. This is what you can find in written statements, and this can be verified if you look at the case file. I don't know whether this is always truth, but you can find it in a written form.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now you seem to have changed the position slightly and you say that -- well, tell us again on whose orders you say this was done.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the written statements, these people explained why they had provided material and equipment because they had been confiscated, and they said that they had given them to Tijanic but not knowing that he would not convey them further. And it was done on the order of Pavkovic and Ojdanic, of Generals Pavkovic and Ojdanic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Aleksic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me whether you know about Buba Bratislava, Buba Morina, what was her position at the time? Am I right in saying she was the commissioner for refugees?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you are right, but she also provided a lot of assistance, a lot of help that had been confiscated from Tijanic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Did you see a document, and let's focus on General Pavkovic, in which General Pavkovic, as the commander of the 3rd Army, provides an authority to the reserve officer and --

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were over a hundred such documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Did you see this one?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not see an order signed by either Ojdanic or Pavkovic. I'm talking about statements, witness statements, and I am talking about the statement by the accused, Tijanic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: We'll move on. Thank you. To save up time to the court and yourself, you spent a great deal of time talking with Mr. Visnjic about the investigations surrounding Stosic and the way the cases came along and so on. I'll read two paragraphs to you, and then please be patient and you will get a chance to answer. As far as Stosic is concerned, in paragraph 25 of your statement you say: "Obrencevic told me that this was the same person as before and that the incident in Decani would be dealt with by other authorities. I said to him, 'Who could these other authorities be? I am the military prosecutor in Pristina. I have jurisdiction over the case.' Obrencevic told me that he would give the case to the military prosecutor at the Pristina Corps command." Wait a minute, please. In paragraph 35 you state: "I came across a grave-site that was discovered near Orahovac. I requested the case be transferred to me. I went with my file to Spasojevic because -- and I expected that we would talk of jurisdiction. I was surprised because he asked me to hand over the case. I refused and told him that I would not do that without an order from Obrencevic." In paragraph 36 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel please repeat what he said.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: -- did you, in fact, state this?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: The time we're talking about is the month of May of 1999. General Obrencevic was the chief military prosecutor. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Milos Spasojevic was the military prosecutor with the Pristina Corps command which -- and was thus, as we were able to see, the first-instance military prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: You were the military prosecutor with the Pristina Military District command?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please call up Prosecution Exhibit P3 -- or rather, P1309. There are two laws there. First we have the law on courts, and we need -- I need the Law on Military Prosecutor's Offices, Articles 18, 19, and 20.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Or rather, Mr. Dorovic, I can already start reading this out to you to save time before it shows up?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter notes that we don't have the text.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Article 18 states: "The first-instance military" --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't catch what the -- can the counsel please read slowly since we don't have it on the screens, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Aleksic, you're going too quickly, because there's no English version on the -- well, there now is a Serb version. Yeah, we now have both. Continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Your Honours. We have the Law on Military Courts which is the first part of this exhibit. What we need is the Law on Military Prosecutor's Offices which is behind this piece of legislation. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's Article 18 of the later section of this exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may be of assistance, I have the text of the Law on Military Prosecutors. Maybe that can be used.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No. We'll find it in a moment. It should be here in the system. No. That's just -- that's just the next page of the same part. It's a second -- there's a later part of this exhibit which also has another Article 18, 19, and 20. The problem, Mr. Aleksic, is we need an e-court number for this, which you haven't given.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Your Honours, if I may assist, they are both in the same exhibit number, P130 -- 1309.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We know that and we now have it I think. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I apologise. In B/C/S, that's page 8 of 11.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can we have your question now, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: You agreed with me about Article 18, and I believe we reached Article 19, paragraph 2.

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have a different text on my screen, something concerning the Tanjug news agency or maybe regulations governing the work of that agency. At any rate, I don't doubt that you indeed read the text accurately.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Is that in English? Is the text in English right? Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, in English I believe we have the right page, do we?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think so, but I don't think think you've got the right one in the Serb.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that the witness will agree with what I have to read out and he will hear the interpretation of what I say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But what is the question you're going to ask him?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I still have to quote one article, Your Honour, and then I will put my question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: So Article 18 says that the military prosecutor of first-instance is responsible to the supreme military prosecutor for his work. Article 19, paragraph 2 says: "The supreme military prosecutor shall direct the work of the first-instance military prosecutor and in this respect may issue mandatory instructions to them." Paragraph 3 of Article 19 reads: "The instructions of the supreme military prosecutor may also concern procedure in specific cases and are binding for military prosecutors of the first instance." Article 20: "The supreme military prosecutor may directly exercise all rights and duties pertaining to the first-instance military prosecutors under the law." And paragraph 2: "The supreme military prosecutor may take over the exercise of certain" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Let's get -- ask the question, Mr. Aleksic. If you need to go back to the documents, we'll go back to them. What's the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dorovic, based on the legal provisions I've just read out and with which you've agreed, I claim that General Obrencevic as the supreme military prosecutor had authorities pursuant to the law, first to provide instructions to you as well as any other military prosecutor to proceed in any case, that he was entitled to take from you or any other prosecutor, for that matter, and hand over that case to any other prosecutor, or he was also entitled to be seized himself of any particular case and of taking any actions in that case. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If he does that in writing or if he formulates this order in writing. He can't do that in a telephone conversation. There has to be a written trace in that given case. If someone who is seized of a case wants to be deprived of that case --

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: This isn't something I asked you. You mention a written order. In paragraph 36 you state that you received a written order order to hand over that case?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But that was later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Later on, but you did not hand over your case before you received a written order.

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never even handed it over. It was taken away from me.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: We will not go into that.

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But that's the gist of it, Mr. Aleksic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Yesterday in your evidence at page 89 of the transcript, lines 24, 25, 26 and on the next page, you spoke of your superior officer, Colonel Nikola Petkovic. You told us that you hold him in high esteem as an officer as and as a person, as a professional. You told us that you worked with him on drafting some regulations.

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's my opinion, indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please call up Prosecution Exhibit P830.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: As you can see, Mr. Dorovic, this is a report on the criminal cases instigated by the military prosecutor's offices against the members of the VJ for violations of the norms of humanitarian law. The date is the 9th of April, 2002, and we have supreme military officer written in the heading. I will read out the first sentence only, which reads: "In the period of 1st of June, 1998, when the terrorist activities in the territory of Kosovo and Metohija escalated until the 27th of June, 1999, when the state of war was annulled, the military judicial organs instituted criminal proceedings against a total of 305 persons for acts violating norms of humanitarian law. Of that number, 38 persons were tried for crimes against humanity and the international law against life and limb and for crimes of personal and moral degradation while proceedings of property crimes were conducted against 267 persons."

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please show the last page of the document in both versions. Let's see who signed the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Is the supreme military prosecutor Colonel Nikola Petkovic the one who signed the document?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You didn't have to waste the time here.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: We do have certain rules that we have to follow, Mr. Dorovic. Let me just ask you this: The last page of the document shows who the document was delivered to, office of the president of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and office of the Federal Ministry of Defence. Therefore, it had nothing to do with the General Staff or any other military institutions. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Why should it have anything to do with it, may I ask?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Well, you cannot ask. They're not there.

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they need not be.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are forgetful of the time when the document was issued. The war had already been finished three years earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Sir, you presented accusations against various institutions in your evidence here --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: If you're moving away from this document, can I ask you, is that supposed to be a record of all prosecutions in Kosovo during the period from -- is it dated 1998 until 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What does it relate to, then? I mean for crimes against humanity and international --

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's every one during that period, is it? Has anybody ever been found guilty of anything?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, we would in that case have to go through the entire document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. If you don't know, then it doesn't matter, because it will arise later. Ms. Moeller, did you want to say something?

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: I just wanted to explain that this list was the list sent to the OSCE when they requested information on these proceedings. That's the document I tendered yesterday under this heading.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, but it has the interesting feature, it doesn't tell you the result of anything, as far as I could tell, unless that's on a later page, and that's 2002. And there's nothing to indicate any prosecutions have been completed by then, which is a rather disturbing thing to see. No doubt it can be clarified later.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I be allowed, Your Honour, to give my observation of the matter?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, if you can assist us factually on it, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Precisely. The figures of 37 and the sum total of the cases processed as well as the date, the 1st of June, 1998, before the start of fighting, this is something that was used in the material sent through the ministry pursuant to a request from the Tribunal. We analysed the document yesterday. It had tables in it. This does not speak of cases that were completed --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Let's go back to the first page, though, please. It's 1st June 1998 until 27th June 1999, and it's the total number of criminal proceedings taken for violations of international humanitarian law during that period.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] According to this report, yes; however, I know that Petkovic as a legalist may have these figures in his records. But they are inaccurate, they are erroneous, because the persons who provided the information did not provide him with accurate information. The fact that some persons were released and their cases aborted are best shown by the fact that you do not find them here, either as persons against whom the case was initiated or who were convicted. And I believe that this report is not complete, although it does -- it did have enough time to obtain all the necessary information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Aleksic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 28 of your statement, you said that at the moment: "The military department of the Belgrade District Court is conducting an investigation against Gojovic, Vukadin Milojevic, and Radenko Miladinovic for abuse of their position and destroying case files." Is that right?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 2005, indeed, there were such proceedings before the supreme military court.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: No, no, I'm asking you something else. You said, and I'm going to read it out once again. Perhaps there's a mistake in the translation. But you said: "In 2005" -- sorry, I misread it. "In 2005, my crime report was accepted, and there is currently an investigation conducted by the military department of the Belgrade district court against Gojovic, Vukadin Milojevic, and Radenko Miladinovic for abuse of their position in destroying case files."

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now, yes, after the ruling of the supreme military court, I can say what --

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Wait a moment --

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now, now, yes. Now proceedings are under way and I can give you the number under which this has taken place. It is KI1/38.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Just wait a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we display on e-court P2759. That is information with regard to a request for assistance. The number is 310. Sent -- sorry. Sent by the Ministry of Foreign Affairs of the Republic of Serbia. In paragraph 2 -- I'm sorry, the English version hasn't appeared on our screens yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 2 it says: "According to the knowledge that the military court in the district of Belgrade has before this court, there are now proceedings, criminal proceedings, against Radomir Gojovic, Vukadin Milojevic, and Radenko Miladinovic for abuse of office and destroying 17 case files on investigations which, according to the information that the Office of the Prosecutor has, were taken from the office on the 30th of May ... " so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note that they do not have the text again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We seem to have two different documents on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, yes, Your Honour, yes. This is a request for assistance that we have in the English version but now we have to look at page 3, the response. So one is the request and then comes the response. Yes, that's right. So what I read out just now is paragraph 2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We've got it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this document, which was written on the 30th of November, shows that the district court in Belgrade and the foreign ministry informed the office of the prosecutor that there are no proceedings of that kind, as the witness spoke of in paragraph 28. In the last paragraph -- now you see the English version. In the last paragraph, it says that in the archives of the district court in Belgrade, there is a case KI2/03 which was brought to an end through a final decision made by the supreme military court, and as for that decision I would like to show that as my next document on e-court, that is P2694 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Before we move from this -- before we move from this document, the matter referred to in the last paragraph, is that something different from what's referred to in the second paragraph?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. This is the same case; however, the district court says that it was archived, that it was resolved, that there was a final decision made. They are saying that there are no live proceedings, but they are saying that it exists in their archives --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's not true, it's not true. Look at the other paragraph just before that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Dorovic, quiet please while I'm speaking. I'm dealing with Mr. Aleksic at the moment.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The last paragraph seems to relate to a suspect called Gojkovic and doesn't look like the same matter as in the second paragraph. It's gone now.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, in paragraph 28 of his statement, the witness says: "The Belgrade District Court is currently conducting an investigation against Gojovic, Vukadin Milojevic, and Radenko Miladinovic for abuse of their position and destroying case files," and in the response it says that there are no such proceedings that are taking place then, that it was brought to a final decision through a ruling of the military court, and the text of the judgement was disclosed by the OTP.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Ms. Moeller.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I just would like to draw the attention of the Court and counsel to the last paragraph which is on the next page. There is another proceeding ongoing. That's the only thing I wanted to say. I wanted to go into that in re-examination, but since the witness got excited, there is one proceeding still ongoing. I just wanted to let Your Honours know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: My reason for asking these questions, if we go back to the page we had before, is that the second paragraph -- one might be forgiven for thinking the second paragraph had been very carefully worded to be confined to the question of whether there was an ongoing criminal procedure. Now, that may not matter very much if the last paragraph refers to the same thing, but on the face of it the last paragraph does not appear to refer to the same thing because it doesn't mention Gojovic -- oh, it does, in fact. It's the third -- yeah, yeah, different order. That's the problem. I'm not reading it in the same way. Right. That's clear now. Thank you. Your next question, Mr. Aleksic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In relation to this, can we please see on e-court P2694.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: So this is the decision of the supreme military court dated the 7th of November, 2003, repelling the complaint of Lakic Dorovic against the decision of the military court; a certain number KV106/03, dated the 25th of June, 2003. And in the introductory part we can see that the names are Vukadin Milojevic, Radenko Miladinovic, and Radomir Gojovic as the persons who are referred to as the accused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's clear. What's your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no question. I'm just saying that that's the document. That is part of the previous document -- well, I'll move on to something else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I just have a few more -- well, I'll try to be as expeditious as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: As you said in your statement and yesterday in the transcript, you said that on the 30th of May you wrote a letter to the commander of the military district of Pristina, Zlatimir Pesic, and we saw that a few times. That is P2754.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we briefly have it back, and my questions have to do with the following:

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Yesterday in the transcript, on page 57, lines 15 through 25, you said that you personally took that document to three addresses, to the commander of the military district, Pesic; then the chief of the security, military security in the military district; and the third copy to Colonel Radosavljevic, who was my immediately superior officer. Now, the last sentence, could you please read the last sentence out for me before your signature.

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "At the same time I have also sent a copy of this complaint, petition, to the security organ of the command of the Pristina Military District and I submitted it to Radosavljevic as well. I did --"

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Wait a moment. You say in this document: "I have also sent a copy of this complaint, petition, to the security organ." You do not refer to Radosavljevic in your own document. That's the only thing I'm referring to.

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But I did provide him with a copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dorovic, do you agree with me that during the war the first-instance prosecutor reports on a daily basis to the prosecutor attached to the army command, as you said in your own statement in paragraph 39. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what we did throughout the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: As far as I understood from your testimony, the representative General Obrencevic, or practically the person who was in charge of the department -- the supreme military prosecutor's department, was Radosavljevic; right?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But I never spoke to him. I never saw him. A few times when he asked for me, I always submitted a report to Radonje Zivkovic, a lieutenant-colonel who was his deputy.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: All right. In relation to that, am I right if I say that during the war all prosecutor's offices and military courts were subjected to the legal department of the ministry and only the supreme military prosecutor's office was detached and was attached to the 3rd Army?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In what sense do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: In terms of submitting reports, reporting to the supreme military prosecutor's office, and in accordance with Article 36 of the Law on Military Prosecutors, where it says what the obligations of the Ministry of Defence are and in relation to the organisation of work in a prosecutor's office.

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely wrong. You are absolutely wrong, Mr. Aleksic. During the war, the legal department had different obligations in terms of statistics and records in terms of cases dealt with. As for information or notification, it is the prosecutors who notified their superior prosecutors, that is to say that we from the ground - if I can put it that way - the offices of the prosecutor attached to commands of the army and then they dealt with the supreme military prosecutor. As far as I know, and I did not work in a court, but as far as I know, from the outside that's the way they worked, too, in the court. So that is the line, but that's not the end of it. And let me tell you one more thing. The legal administration of the General Staff organised the complete work and also -- this is a very important thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Please, you were responsible to the supreme military prosecutor as a first-instance prosecutor. We agree on that?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The legal department did not have competences during the war -- I mean, I'm talking about the legal department of the ministry. General Gojovic created all of this work --

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Please, please, let us deal with something else now. In paragraph 44 of your statement you talk about a meeting dated the -- that took place on the 24th of November, 1999, and in your statement you say that Pavkovic's logistics assistant chaired the meeting and you say who the attendees were. Also present were General Obrencevic, Gojkovic, the assistant for logistics, and General Uzelac.

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not what I said. I never said that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Well, please look at paragraph 44. The first sentence: "The meeting was led by an assistant of Pavkovic for logistics."

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Then -- sorry, 44, yes. My mistake.

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, please do not combine paragraphs. If we are talking --

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Sorry, I have already apologised. Paragraph 44.

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I make no reference to that there. It's not true. The generals before that had two meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dorovic, please read the first sentence to me. "The meeting was led by an assistant of Pavkovic for logistics."

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's the way it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 41 you say: "General Pavkovic gave instructions for having this meeting organised. I know that because I have the written order from Pavkovic." What kind of order?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is an order to have a meeting held where these questions would be discussed, and it exists in the files of the supreme military court, 269.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: So Pavkovic's assistant for logistics chaired the meeting. Could you tell me what the name is of that officer?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was Dasic. He was there in the beginning. However, General Uzelac was the person who was actually in charge of the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: You said that yesterday, but now I'm reading the statement to you. The statement says: "... led by the assistant of Pavkovic for logistics ..." --

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The introductory part, five minutes or something. I don't know. I think it's Dasic. But at any rate I know that he was introduced as the person in charge of logistics, and then the meeting was chaired by General Uzelac.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Thank you for that explanation. Also in the transcript from yesterday, when you were saying something else, on two places, lines 19 and 25 on page 28, you repeated twice that the Chief of General Staff during 1999 was General Pavkovic. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps I made a mistake there. Actually, I'm not certain of the dates. I know that chiefs were appointed and relieved of duty --

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: I'm not asking about chiefs. Yesterday -- you said that yesterday. General Pavkovic, was he Chief of General Staff in 1999?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure about that. I think that during the war he was -- well --

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: All right. So this meeting of the 24th of November, he was the Chief of General Staff and it was his assistant who chaired this meeting?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There's an order --

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you if I'm right. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There's an order.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: With the signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please see on e-court now 4D163. That's the last page, I believe. It exists in B/C/S and -- yes, yes, in the B/C/S, it's the one-but-last. In English it's page number - I am sorry about this - number 6.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: And we have number 8 here and then these two tables where it says: "Transferred and assigned according to peacetime establishment to the position of Chief of General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia in the year 2000, the 23rd of February, year 2000." Can you see it --

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Rather, can we see the previous page in the B/C/S version so that the witness could see it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We don't -- is this to prove when Mr. Pavkovic became Chief of the General Staff? It's a matter of -- it's in the indictment as a matter that the Prosecution have conceded. This isn't something you need to go about, this elaborate exercise of trying to prove.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just put to the witness that he's wrong. We don't need all this.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Yesterday, on the issue of this meeting, we were looking at an overview of confiscated and taken vehicles. That's P2752. At pages 74 to 76, you spoke about this, and on page 75, line 20, when answering to a question by His Honour Judge Bonomy to illustrate in an example how it was for the -- possible for the army to take 92 vehicles for purposes other than military purposes, you give your answer on page 75, line 20, by mentioning 10.000 vehicles from Vogosca, Sarajevo, and Banja Luka. You speak of the vehicles and of a time-period which was considerably earlier than 1998 or 1999. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The question was whether the army had been bringing in vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: We have an indictment and are dealing with the time-period between the 24th of March and June 1999. The incident involving vehicles from Vogosca was some seven or eight years earlier.

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that if need be I can provide even a thousand examples.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Please, we have the table here. Yesterday you spoke of the 1st Army when replying to the Judge. Here we can see that the 2nd Army also had vehicles, as did the air force and the ground forces and security administration. Are all these groups part of the army? Can you perhaps provide us with an example that would involve these other elements of the army.

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean the other ones?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Which ones?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The command of the 2nd Army was bringing in from the Dubrovnik frontline in an organised fashion vehicles for General Strugar, and this was well-known.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: I apologise. I told you a moment ago that we are interested in the year 1999. There is no General Strugar.

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean a case involving vehicles from Kosovo being brought in?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: I was asking you about these other groups.

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't see what you're asking me.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: About the 1st Army?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Dorovic, just try to listen to what you're being asked. These questions relate to the 1st and the 2nd Army. Generally speaking, it would appear they weren't in Kosovo. If you look at the date on the document, you'll see it's about 1999. So with that background, would you listen carefully to the question, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Yesterday you said that, despite the fact the tables were presented this way, that all these vehicles came from Kosovo, and then His Honour asked you about the 1st Army and then you didn't. And then I'm asking you now to give me an example that would involve the 2nd Army or any other formation where a vehicle was seized and that it had to do with that time-period.

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I filed criminal reports. You forget that I got into conflict with security organs when I asked my prosecutors to give those vehicles back, not to use them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: But that was in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely. Should I talk about Kosovo or do you not want me to talk about Kosovo now? And then there's another matter involving vehicles being pulled out of Kosovo --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Why can't you just listen to the question and try to answer it? Just listen again to what you're being asked. You're being asked -- let's take the example of the 2nd Army, and if you look at this table, you'll see 59 private cars in the first column. Got that? Have you got that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, give us an example of a legitimate way in which, in 1999, the 2nd Army, wherever it was, probably not Kosovo, would take one of these 59 vehicles from its owner or from wherever it was. Give us an example so we can understand this concept that falls into that column.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You said legally take or legally taken?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Legally, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I disregard what was considered to be a material duty, what was exercised by military departments, aside from that, I wouldn't know of a single case where the army took vehicles in a legitimate way, in accordance with the law. But the vehicles that the army took as part of the material obligation of the owners, this was prescribed by law and constituted a legal procedure. What we are talking about here are vehicles that were unlawfully taken to Belgrade, and the question was raised as to what to do with these unlawfully seized vehicles. And these 213 vehicles --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Dorovic, are you saying that this document relates to vehicles which were taken illegally, this particular document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Absolutely, Mr. President. That was the very reason why it had to be decided what to do with the vehicles.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Who compiled this document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I saw the document for the first time when the generals tasked me with preparing that note. I believe it was drafted by the chief of the traffic administration, General Uzelac, or his people but I'm not sure about that. When the meeting started, he was the one who personally gave us this table in addition to other material. I had already had this document because at the previous two meetings the generals didn't have the table whilst I had; I got it there. This was another example. General Uzelac asked his associates to distribute a set of materials to all those present, including this table. I'm not really sure whether he himself authored the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So the answer is: None of these were seized legitimately. Mr. Aleksic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 46 you speak of a draft document following this meeting, and that on the 16th of December, the then-president of the supreme military court signed document P2750 which you had drafted. You commented on one of the paragraphs, I believe it was paragraph 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please call up P2750.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: In your statement you say on this very issue, in paragraph 46: "I drafted the document and this is another piece of evidence showing that the supreme military court refused to provide an alibi for the Yugoslav Army to keep the goods and vehicles after the war." Mr. Dorovic, we said who sent the document and to whom. I will read the first paragraph below the heading which says: "With reference to your" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, no, let's hear the question first before we decide whether we need to go through this palaver every time a question's asked.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My apologies. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dorovic, I put it to you that what you said does not transpire from this document, but rather that paragraphs 2 and 4 of this document, which have to do with the federal government, the supreme military court provides two possible ways of solving this request, as I read it, in reference to the draft order on the return of the vehicles and not on retaining these vehicles. And if you disagree with me about the two ways of solving the problem, then I will have to read out paragraphs 2 and 3 to you, with the permission of the Court, of course. In particular, paragraph 3 says: "Having in mind the possible consequences, not just material ones, it may be best if the final decision about all of this is made by the federal government in the same manner in which this matter will be dealt with in relation to the vehicles at our disposal." This is the opinion pursuant to a request asking how to proceed. I'm not saying that the supreme military court is providing an alibi but, rather, two possible ways of solving this problem, and that is all which concerns this matter.

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And what is your question for me?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Well, I put it to you that contrary to what is contained in this statement -- in this document, paragraph 3.

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps the Tribunal should also be given the possibility to analyse the draft decision as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Well, you see, we don't have that. I am presenting you this.

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The draft decision says that the vehicles should be kept and distributed, but this decision was never publicised.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: This decision that you're talking about, was it ever signed by anyone?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have just told you that it was never signed, but this is the way it was acted upon --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Dorovic, you have a great ability for hijacking the proceedings. Could you just answer the question, which is that the document doesn't support what you say in your statement, that this is an example showing that the supreme military court refused to provide an alibi for the VJ to keep the goods and vehicles. Now, what's your comment on that suggestion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wanted to highlight the fact that the point this document makes when you analyse it in its entirety is that the supreme military court suggested that no specific enactment be made. This decision, which was the subject of the analysis and which in fact stated that the vehicles should be distributed to those who had obtained them in the first place, regardless of the fact it was done unlawfully, and all of this in accordance with the regulations valid in 1991. If you analyse -- or rather, the analysis itself is based on that very decision --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Dorovic, you have said that this is an example of the supreme military court refusing to provide an alibi for the VJ to keep the goods and vehicles. Now, where do we see that? Tell us which part of the text is it -- makes it clear that this is a refusal to help the VJ to keep the goods.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Those sections of the document where the president of the supreme military court says that no special enactment should be issued because it is pointless and that the decision about this matter should be taken by the government which will take care -- or rather, this should be analysed in conjunction with the fact that a large number of these vehicles were in possession of the ministry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Aleksic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dorovic, I will try to complete my cross-examination. You speak of the events of the 30th of May. I will give you the number of the paragraph or -- yes, that's paragraph 31. You state there: "One day two military" -- or rather-- my apologies. "On the 30th of May a military police officer and two military police officers came to my office. They offended me and I beat one of them up and the others fled. I then wrote a report about the incident." Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Beaten up, well, I said that I had the upper hand.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: We'll get to that. Mr. Dorovic, tell me, because of this event on the 30th of May, was a criminal proceeding instituted against you before the military court attached to the 3rd Army command?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: On the 11th of June, was a decision taken on an investigation carried out against you?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about the date, but yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: This is exhibit -- I would like to read one part of this decision which says-- that's 4D165.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My apologies, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: The disposition of this decision says against you -- an investigation was conducted against you because there was reasonable suspicion to believe that as a military prosecutor in Pristina on the 30th of May at around 2200 hours whilst in your official office you hurt severely Dragoljub --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't hear the last name.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: -- your deputy prosecutor in Pristina by drawing out your pistol and telling the aggrieved parties, or rather, saying something disparaging to them and then you knocked that person down and kicked him in the head repeatedly with your military boots. When a police officer arrived to intervene you said, Scram, all of you, I will kill you all. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you asking me whether you read this correctly? Yes, that's true. Now, if you're asking me whether this is true, I will tell you right away, this is not true. Something that lends support to what I say is the final decision. Six hearings were held --

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Tell me the upshot.

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After six hearings were heard, the prosecutor dropped charges for what you've just read out.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Tell me when this was and who was the prosecutor involved.

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you want me to, I can show you the court documentation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: For which crime?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Grievous bodily harm, but the charges were not dropped and it was delegated to the military court, or rather, the department in Belgrade where two hearings were held.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: I have to interrupt you. We're all very tired. I'm not asking you for how many criminal offences. I'm just asking you is -- are these criminal proceedings that were initiated ex officio against you, are they still pending?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I told you, I received a new indictment after the first hearing. Then I was supposed to appear at the trial in order for it to end. I talked about this yesterday. Once again I will write a request to have this direct confrontation done with.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dorovic, can you answer my question. Are there criminal proceedings pending against you in Belgrade for any criminal offence which can be prosecuted ex officio?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was told that it was not ongoing because the district military prosecutor dropped the charges for the remaining allegations which was the conflict with the police officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I will finish soon.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: When was it that you learned that the prosecutor dropped the charges for all these actions? When did you learn about it?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I raised the issue of my promotion. It was just recently, in the month of March.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: You mean in the current month of 2007?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 1st or the 2nd.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One more question, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 57 you state, among other things: "The decision on my promotion was revoked at the last moment." Can you tell me who revoked the decision and who drafted the revoking decision and at which point in time this happened.

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you for asking me. I will tell you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Tell me which month and which year are involved.

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It took place on that same day when I celebrated my promotion on the 4th, or rather, no, on the 5th of June, 1999. That's what I'm referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: You said that you were in detention on the 4th. How could you be promoted on the 5th and you had submitted your resignation on the 30th?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm telling you upon my full responsibility that on the 5th of June in the morning I was celebrating my promotion with my generals. I can show you the document, and can I have the permission of the Tribunal to show you the document authored by the supreme military prosecutor Colonel Petkovic where he gives a written confirmation thereof. My generals, who celebrated with me in the morning, can confirm this. In the afternoon they were asked to help to destroy me.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us who wrote this decision to promote you during a time of war. Where is this decision?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, the decision, no. I told you that it was withdrawn at the last moment. It was a decree by the president of the republic, the late Slobodan Milosevic, upon the proposal of the supreme military prosecutor. You have these documents, Mr. Aleksic. You can consult them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Let us finish. We are at the end of the day. On the 5th of June, 1999, you were supposed to be promoted, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: LAKIC DOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A decree is being served on a person. There is a certain procedure to be followed. I was told that it was signed and that we were only waiting for it to be officially served. It was still a time of war. I don't know how long it would take such documents normally to arrive, but there is a document to that effect and you can consult it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, unfortunately, I won't be able to finish now. I will need ten minutes more and by your leave, I will then be able to complete my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, we have to interrupt again, Mr. Dorovic, because there are other court proceedings here this afternoon. We have no more time, albeit we would like to continue to complete this. So you have to return again tomorrow morning to continue your evidence, and that again will be at 9.00. Meanwhile, can you please leave the courtroom with the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: One matter I want to address just before we leave, Ms. Moeller, and it's really to make sure the message is passed on. This morning with Mr. Hannis we discussed the question of any further documents that the Prosecution seek to have admitted in the language we use here from the bar table. And the -- the discussion was confined to the evidence of Mr. Coo. And Mr. Hannis explained how he intended to deal with that. If there are documents relating to any other matters other than those that will be dealt with by him and it's intended to make a motion for them to be admitted as stand-alone documents, then there has to be a deadline for that. Now, are you aware of whether there are any other documents that is intended to submit in that form?

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I think there is a small amount of documents where we may have another motion and it's currently being worked on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: When will that be filed?

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: As soon as possible, of course, but that won't help you. So we're aiming at maybe -- yes, we're aiming towards the end of the week, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Not good enough, Ms. Moeller. Anything of that nature has to be in our hands no later than the end of this week. To enable this -- the Defence to have an opportunity to address the issue, we can't allow any more time than that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: We will do our very best, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: This has been ongoing --

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- since the pre-trial stage. This isn't something that's just arising now. Unless it relates to documents that have only recently been received. But so far as others are concerned --.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- it's a long outstanding issue.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Yes. Part of the documents which we intend to file something on are indeed documents where we very recently got the translation only. Others are the ones that we selected from a very serious cut of our exhibit list and the boiling down of documents that we really need. But we will seek to file something by Friday, as you ordered us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Tomorrow we sit from 9.00 to 1.45.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 15th day of March, 2007, at 9.00 a.m. 16 17 18 19 20 21 22 23 24
